e-rc-technique.aiPrompt: Create 3 IBPS Clerk PRELIMS level reading comprehension sets. Each: one 320-400 word passage in four or five clear paragraphs on Indian banking, RBI policy, digital public infrastructure, climate finance or rural livelihoods, written in a policy-commentary register with at least one 'However' or 'Yet' turn and at least four specific figures, dates or proper nouns. Follow each passage with NINE questions, each having exactly FIVE options labelled (a) to (e). Compose the nine as: 2 vocabulary questions ('most similar in meaning to X as used in the passage' and 'most opposite in meaning to Y as used in the passage'), where the passage's sense of the word differs from its most common dictionary sense and that common sense appears as a distractor; 4 direct-detail questions each answerable from one identifiable sentence, with two distractors that are close paraphrases differing in a single qualifier; 1 inference question where the correct option is traceable to a specific line or contrast and one distractor is true in the real world but unsupported by the text; 1 main idea or suitable title question with two distractors that are accurate about a single paragraph only and one that is broader than anything the passage claims; and 1 multi-statement question with three Roman-numeral statements and combination options ending in 'None of these'. Then give an answer key that, for every question, quotes the exact line from the passage that decides it, and names why each rejected option fails. Also state which of the nine you classify as anchored versus unanchored.
e-rc-technique.blockPlan: This is the largest English block and it should have the largest share of the English hour throughout. Weeks 1-4, 30 minutes daily: one passage untimed with the full apparatus written out — stem sort into circles and squares, paragraph tags during the read, and after each question the line number that gave you the answer. Accuracy first; ignore the clock entirely in this phase. Weeks 5-10, 35 minutes daily: two passages, the first on an 8-minute timer and the second untimed for review, plus a written error log classified only as 'answered from memory instead of locating', 'inference with no supporting line', 'theme option too narrow' or 'vocabulary taken from dictionary not passage' — four categories, because a longer taxonomy will not get used. Weeks 11 onward to Prelims, 30 minutes daily: three timed passages every other day alternating with a review day on the error log. Post-Prelims through 27 December, shift to Mains length: two 350-500 word passages per session at 7.5-8.5 minutes each, four days a week, since Mains RC carries a much larger share of a section that decides the merit list. Keep RC daily rather than in blocks — reading speed and the tagging habit both decay quickly and neither can be rebuilt in the final fortnight.
e-rc-technique.bookRef: Objective General English by S.P. Bakshi (Arihant) — Part C, 'Objective Comprehension'
e-rc-technique.websiteRef: For daily practice sets, bankersadda.com and careerpower.in publish IBPS Clerk pattern RC quizzes. For reading stamina and the vocabulary these passages actually recycle, read the editorial and business-comment pages of a national daily every day — 15 minutes of policy-register prose does more for RC speed than an extra practice set, because the passages are drawn from that register.
e-rc-technique.weightageNote: Reading Comprehension is the largest single English block in both phases, and this note states the counts factually rather than ranking topics. In IBPS Clerk Prelims 2025, RC appeared in every one of the 8 publicly analysed shifts of 4-5 October at 8-10 of the 30 English questions (Prelims ran 4 shifts per day on 4, 5 and 11 October 2025, so those 8 are a partial but consistent sample). In Mains 2025, the IBPS Guide shift tables give RC at 16 of 40 on 29 November and 15 of 40 on 2 December, both across two passages; Career Power's count for 29 November is lower at about 12. Coaching shift tables are reconstructed from candidate recall and disagree, so the defensible statement is that Mains RC ran at roughly 12-16 of 40 English questions in 2025 — treat 12-16 as the planning range and do not quote a single figure. Two practical consequences: RC is worth a disproportionate share of your English preparation time in both phases, and because Mains decides the final merit while Prelims is only qualifying, the Mains-length practice after 11 October 2026 matters more per hour than the Prelims-length practice before it.

e-rc-econ.topicName: RC on economic and banking themes
e-rc-econ.whatItIs: RC passages drawn from editorials on monetary policy, inflation, banking regulation, NPAs, fiscal deficit, digital payments and financial inclusion. A distinct topic because the vocabulary is a closed set and the argument structures repeat — which means these passages can be made your fastest, not your hardest.
e-rc-econ.coreMethod:
1. PRE-LOAD THE LEXICON. Roughly 120 terms cover 90% of these passages. Learn them before the exam so you never spend reading time decoding: inflation, deflation, disinflation, stagflation, repo rate, reverse repo, liquidity, monetary tightening/easing, fiscal deficit, revenue deficit, NPA, bad loan, haircut, provisioning, recapitalisation, moratorium, disbursement, credit offtake, CASA, capital adequacy, systemic risk, moral hazard, subsidy, austerity, stimulus, GDP, GVA, current account deficit, FDI, FII, depreciation, tariff, protectionism, demand-side, supply-side, capex, informal sector, financial inclusion, microfinance, insolvency, IBC, securitisation, yield, bond, benchmark, MCLR, priority sector lending, disintermediation, arbitrage, volatility, headwinds, tailwinds.
2. NAME THE ARGUMENT SHAPE in the first 30 seconds. In practice there are only five: (a) problem -> cause -> consequence -> recommendation; (b) policy announced -> benefits claimed -> limitations; (c) two-sided debate -> author leans one way at the end; (d) data/trend -> explanation -> outlook; (e) historical comparison -> present situation -> lesson. Once you have named the shape you know exactly where the central-idea and author's-view answers sit.
3. LOCATE THE AUTHOR'S OPINION. In economic editorials it is almost always in the final paragraph, or in the sentence immediately after the first strong contrast word. Mark that sentence during your single read.
4. DETAIL QUESTIONS here are usually cause-effect ('what, according to the author, is the reason for X'). Find X in the passage, then read the sentence BEFORE it — in this register the cause almost always precedes the effect.
5. TREAT NUMBERS AS LANDMARKS, NOT DATA. Statistics in these passages are decoration about 80% of the time. Circle where they are so you can jump back, but do not read them carefully and never do arithmetic.
6. TRACK WHO IS SPEAKING. These passages quote critics, economists, the RBI, the government and industry. Every time you see 'critics argue', 'the government claims', 'economists warn', put a small mark. Author's-view questions are built on candidates confusing a quoted view with the author's.
tricks: Read one editorial a day from The Hindu business page, Business Standard, Livemint or the Indian Express 'Explained' section. The point is not vague English improvement — it is that the vocabulary becomes automatic, which turns a 4-minute passage into a 2-minute one. That is the entire return on the habit.
Keep a one-page 'econ RC glossary' of only the terms that actually slowed you down. After about 30 days it stops growing. That plateau is your proof the habit has done its job.
The sentence after the FIRST 'however' in an economic editorial is very often the thesis. Read that one sentence twice and the rest once.

For 'the author's attitude towards <policy>', read only the modal verbs: 'must', 'should', 'needs to' signal advocacy; 'may', 'might', 'appears', 'could' signal hedging; 'failed to', 'little more than', 'at best', 'falls short' signal criticism. You can answer a tone question from modals alone in 20 seconds.

Reject any option that upgrades a correlation into a causation. If the passage says two things 'are associated with' or 'coincided with' each other and the option says one 'causes' the other, that option is wrong. This single check resolves a large share of economic-RC inference questions.

Because the vocabulary is closed, economic passages should become your FASTEST RC type within six weeks of daily editorial reading. If they are still your slowest after that, the glossary habit is not being done properly.
traps: Using your General Awareness knowledge to answer. You may know the current repo rate; the passage may be from three years ago. Every answer must come from the text.
Confusing a critic's argument with the author's position. Economic editorials quote opponents at length, and 'Critics argue that...' is not the author's view.

Assuming a negative-sounding passage means the author opposes the policy. Very often the author supports it and is listing risks — the tone question then has 'cautiously supportive' or 'analytical' as the answer, not 'critical'.
Getting bogged down in a statistics-heavy paragraph. Skim it; the questions rarely require the numbers.
Mistaking a recommendation for a fact: 'the government should recapitalise the banks' is not the same as 'the government recapitalised the banks', and detail questions exploit exactly this gap.
Picking the technically correct economics answer over the one the passage states. Your knowledge is a reading-speed advantage, never an answering shortcut.
Assuming every economic passage is anti-government or pro-reform. The stance varies by source and the tone question punishes assumptions.
e-rc-econ.timeTarget: Prelims set (400 words, 8-9 questions): 5.5 to 6.5 minutes. Mains set (600-700 words, 10 questions): 8 to 9 minutes. Once the lexicon is automatic these should run 30 to 60 seconds faster than an equivalent social-theme passage.
e-rc-econ.masteryCheck: You can read a 500-word Business Standard or Hindu business editorial with no dictionary and, in under 3 minutes, state its thesis and the author's stance in two sentences — on 4 days out of 5. Test this by writing the two sentences down, then re-reading the editorial to check you were right.
questionPatterns: Central idea or title of a monetary-policy or banking-reform passage.
'What, according to the author, is the primary reason for <the problem>?' — cause-effect detail.
'Which of the following would the author most likely support?' — author's view, answered from the final paragraph.
'What does the author imply about <the policy>?' — inference built on a contrast connector.
Tone: analytical, critical, cautiously optimistic, objective, concerned.
Synonym/antonym of a highlighted economic or general term used in a specific sense.
'Which of the following statements is NOT true according to the passage' with three statements built from different paragraphs.
Occasionally a question distinguishing the author's view from a quoted critic's view.
e-rc-econ.searchQuery: reading comprehension economy banking passage bank exam practice with answers inference author view
e-rc-econ.aiPrompt: Act as an IBPS Clerk paper-setter. Write ONE original 550-word passage in the register of an Indian newspaper business editorial on a banking or macroeconomic theme (choose from: NPAs and provisioning, monetary policy transmission, financial inclusion and microfinance, digital payments and cash usage, MSME credit, or inflation targeting). Follow the structure: problem -> cause -> consequence -> author's recommendation. Deliberately include one paragraph quoting CRITICS whose view differs from the author's, and include at least three statistics. Highlight three words in bold. Then write 10 IBPS-format questions with five options each: 1 central idea, 3 cause-effect detail, 1 question that specifically tests whether I can distinguish the critics' view from the author's, 2 inference, 1 tone, 2 vocabulary on the bold words. Include at least one wrong option per inference question that upgrades a correlation in the passage into a causation. Then give an answer key quoting the exact justifying line for each answer and explaining every wrong option in one line. Do not reveal answers before the key.
e-rc-econ.bookRef: No grammar book covers this well — it is a reading habit, not a chapter. Use daily editorials plus previous-year IBPS papers. If you want a single reference for the vocabulary, S.P. Bakshi 'Objective General English' Part B (Words with Meanings, Synonyms and Antonyms) helps with the general terms but not the economic ones; build the economic glossary yourself from your reading.
e-rc-econ.websiteRef: The Hindu (thehindu.com) business and editorial pages; Business Standard; Livemint; The Indian Express 'Explained' section. For practice sets: PracticeMock (practicemock.com), Bankersadda (bankersadda.com), Oliveboard (oliveboard.in), SmartKeeda Testzone.
e-rc-econ.weightageNote: Economic and banking themes are one of the two most common RC topic families in IBPS (alongside social themes). Expect at least one such passage across your Prelims shift and Mains paper — roughly 5-9 marks in Prelims and 6-13 in Mains, depending on how many sets share the theme.
e-rc-econ.blockPlan: 15m: read one business editorial, and write down every term you had to slow down on into the glossary page — nothing else. 20m untimed: one 550-word economic passage worked fully, marking the author's-opinion sentence and every 'critics say' attribution before answering. 20m timed: one economic RC set at 6.5 minutes, then one at 6 minutes. 5m: revise the glossary page aloud, and note whether it grew today — a shrinking growth rate is the metric that matters.

e-rc-social.whatItIs: Passages on education, gender, health, environment, urbanisation, migration, inequality, technology-and-society, mental health and employment. More abstract vocabulary, longer sentences and a heavier inference load than economic passages — and at Clerk level this is also where narrative and story-based passages appear.
e-rc-social.coreMethod:
1. SEPARATE CLAIM FROM EVIDENCE. Social passages are claim-driven rather than data-driven. As you read, keep two things distinct: the CLAIM (a 'should', 'must' or 'is failing' sentence) and the EVIDENCE (anecdotes, examples, studies). Nearly every inference question in a social passage tests whether you can tell them apart.
2. USE PARAGRAPH OPENERS AS A MAP. Social-theme passages are more likely than economic ones to be organised one-idea-per-paragraph, so the first sentence of each paragraph is a reliable index. Read those sentences with extra attention on your single pass.
3. HANDLE ABSTRACT WORDS BY READING FORWARD, NOT STOPPING. When you hit a term you do not know (stigma, precarity, hegemony, marginalisation, agency), do not stop. Social writing almost always restates or exemplifies the abstract term in the very next sentence. Read on and the meaning arrives free.
4. FOR NARRATIVE PASSAGES (common at Clerk level, rare at PO level), track four things only: who, what changed, why it changed, and what the point of the story is. Questions are mostly detail plus 'what does the passage suggest about the character'. Do not look for a thesis — narrative passages have a moral, not an argument.
5. LONG-SENTENCE DISCIPLINE. These passages use 35-45 word sentences with multiple clauses. Read to the first full stop, then name the subject and the main verb in your head before continuing. If you cannot name them, re-read that one sentence — not the paragraph.
6. ATTACK ORDER: vocabulary -> detail -> theme -> tone -> inference. Same order as general RC, but budget more time for inference here, because social passages typically carry 2-3 inference questions rather than 1.
tricks: Social passages hedge heavily, so hedged options win. In inference questions, options containing 'may', 'often', 'tends to', 'in some cases', 'can' are more likely correct, and absolutes ('all', 'never', 'always', 'none') more likely wrong. This signal is stronger in social passages than in economic ones.

Check every option for the quantifier switch. If the passage says 'many women' or 'some migrants' and the option says 'women' or 'all migrants', that single-word generalisation is the most common wrong-option construction in social RC. Scanning options for this alone catches several marks per paper.
For 'the author would most likely agree with', pick the option that restates the passage's central claim in WEAKER language. Correct answers are almost never stronger than the passage itself.

Tone options for social passages cluster in a small set: concerned, critical, sympathetic, analytical, objective. If the author uses emotive language about people affected -> sympathetic or concerned. If about institutions or policy -> critical. Twenty seconds, decided from adjectives alone.

The opening anecdote is never the thesis. In social passages the story is an illustration and the actual claim arrives one or two paragraphs later — go looking for it there when a central-idea question appears.

Read The Hindu op-eds and Indian Express editorials on social subjects specifically. Bank RC passages copy this exact sentence architecture, so familiarity with the register translates directly into reading speed.
traps: Moralising — picking the option that sounds most socially virtuous rather than the one the passage actually states. Option-writers exploit this deliberately and it is the defining trap of social RC.
Answering a 'what does the author suggest' question with your own opinion on the social issue. You have opinions about education and gender; the passage may not share them.
Anecdote-as-thesis: treating the opening story as the main idea and choosing a title based on it.
Losing the subject of a long multi-clause sentence by the time you reach the verb, then answering from a half-parsed sentence.
Assuming that criticism of a policy means opposition to the goal. An author can support universal education and criticise how it is being delivered — and the tone question hinges on that distinction.
Treating a narrative passage like an argumentative one and hunting for a thesis that does not exist.
Over-reading inference questions. Even in social passages the correct inference is one small step from the text, never two.

Skipping social passages because the vocabulary looks harder. The vocabulary is more abstract but the logic is simpler than in economic passages — the questions are usually more directly traceable to lines.
e-rc-social.timeTarget: Prelims set (400 words, 8-9 questions): 6 to 7 minutes — expect this to run 30 seconds slower than an economic set because of the extra inference questions. Mains set (600-700 words): 8.5 to 9.5 minutes. Inference questions here: 50-60 seconds each.
e-rc-social.masteryCheck: On a fresh social-theme passage with 8 questions including 3 inference questions, you score 6 or more in under 7 minutes, and on every inference question you got right you can point to the specific line the inference was one step away from.
questionPatterns: Central idea or title, where the opening anecdote is planted as a decoy title.
'What can be inferred about <the group discussed>?' — usually 2 of these per set.
Detail questions on a study, survey or example mentioned in the passage.
'The author's attitude towards <the institution/policy> is best described as...' — tone.
'Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a reason for <the problem>?'
Synonym or antonym of an abstract highlighted word used in a specific sense.
'What does the passage suggest about the character/protagonist?' — for narrative passages.
Multi-statement questions where one statement over-generalises what the passage said about 'some' or 'many'.
e-rc-social.searchQuery: reading comprehension social issues passage bank exam practice inference tone author attitude
e-rc-social.aiPrompt: Act as an IBPS Clerk paper-setter. Write ONE original 500-word passage in the register of an Indian newspaper op-ed on a social theme (choose from: girls' school dropout rates, urban migrant housing, mental health stigma, air pollution and public health, or the digital divide in rural education). Structure it as: opening anecdote about one individual -> broader claim -> supporting evidence including one survey statistic -> counter-consideration -> author's position. Use 'many', 'some' and 'often' where you make general statements, never 'all'. Highlight three abstract words in bold. Then write 8 IBPS-format questions with five options each: 1 title question where one wrong option is based only on the opening anecdote, 2 detail, 3 inference, 1 tone, 1 vocabulary on a bold word. In each inference question include one wrong option that changes 'many' or 'some' into 'all', and one wrong option that is socially virtuous-sounding but unsupported by the text. Then give an answer key quoting the exact justifying line for each answer and explaining every wrong option in one line. Do not reveal answers before the key.
e-rc-social.bookRef: Not a book topic — built through reading and timed practice. S.P. Bakshi, 'Objective General English', Part C (Objective Comprehension) gives the question-type grounding; volume comes from previous-year papers and daily op-ed reading.
e-rc-social.websiteRef: The Hindu op-ed page; The Indian Express editorials; Down To Earth for environment passages. For practice: PracticeMock (practicemock.com), Bankersadda (bankersadda.com), Oliveboard (oliveboard.in), IBPS Guide (ibpsguide.com), Testbook (testbook.com) previous-year sets.
e-rc-social.weightageNote: Alongside economic themes, one of the two dominant RC topic families. In a typical Prelims shift with two RC sets, one is usually social or narrative. Worth roughly 4-9 marks in Prelims and 6-13 in Mains depending on set composition.
e-rc-social.blockPlan: 15m: read one social op-ed and write its claim in one sentence and its evidence in one sentence — this drill is the entire skill for this topic. 20m untimed: one 500-word social passage worked fully, and for every inference question write down the line it is one step away from. 20m timed: two social-theme sets at 7 and 6.5 minutes. 5m: log misses specifically as 'moralised' (chose the virtuous option) versus 'over-generalised' (missed a some/all switch) — these two account for most losses here.

e-rc-long.whatItIs: A 600-800 word passage with 8-10 questions in the Mains paper, where English is 40 questions in 35 minutes and every mark counts toward the final merit list. RC is about 13 of those 40 marks, so this cannot be skipped the way a Prelims set can.
e-rc-long.coreMethod:
1. BUDGET. 9 minutes for a 10-question long set — about 54 seconds per question, of which the passage itself consumes 3.5 to 4 minutes. Set this cap before you start and honour it.
2. READ THE PASSAGE FIRST, NOT THE QUESTIONS. This is the opposite of the Prelims rule and it matters. With 700 words and 8-10 questions, reading stems first costs more than it saves, and the theme, tone and inference questions all require a whole-passage view anyway.
3. PARAGRAPH TAGGING — the core technique. After each paragraph, write a 2-3 word label in the margin: 'P1: the problem', 'P2: RBI response', 'P3: critique', 'P4: what next'. Five seconds per paragraph, and it saves 60+ seconds on every subsequent detail question because you jump straight to the right paragraph instead of scanning 700 words. This is the highest-return habit in Mains English.
4. ORDER OF ATTEMPT within the set: vocabulary -> detail (jump using your tags) -> central idea -> tone -> inference -> multi-statement questions LAST. Multi-statement items are the most time-expensive per mark in the entire paper.
5. MULTI-STATEMENT HANDLING (I/II/III, 'which of the following is/are true'): evaluate each statement independently against its tagged paragraph, write T or F for each on the rough sheet, and only then look at the options. Never eliminate options directly — you will end up re-reading the passage.
6. DETAIL-QUESTION ORDERING. In Mains long passages, detail questions follow passage order roughly 70% of the time. If Q3's answer came from paragraph 2, start Q4 in paragraph 2 or 3. Never restart from the top.
7. TRIAGE BETWEEN SETS. If the Mains paper has two RC sets and one passage is opaque after paragraph 1, do the other set first and return. The whole 35 minutes is yours to allocate within English — there is no sub-sectional lock.
8. ABANDON RULE. Hard cap of 10 minutes on a single long set. At 10 minutes, answer what you have, mark the rest, and move on. Twelve minutes on one RC set is how candidates leave 15 questions unattempted.
tricks: Paragraph tagging is the trick. Nothing else in Mains RC returns as much time. Practise it until the labels appear without conscious effort — five words per paragraph, no full sentences.

Go directly to the last paragraph for any 'the author's conclusion/suggestion/recommendation is' question. In long editorial passages this answer is in the final paragraph well over half the time, and you do not need to recall anything.

For highlighted-word vocabulary questions at Mains (which often test a secondary meaning), substitute each option into the ORIGINAL sentence and read it mentally. Wrong options usually break the grammar or the register even when the dictionary meaning seems close — much faster than trying to recall definitions.

For 'which of the following would weaken/strengthen the author's argument', pick the option that attacks the CAUSAL LINK, not the one that simply disagrees with the conclusion. Options that merely contradict the conclusion are the standard decoy.
Use the contrast connectors as a tagging shortcut. If a paragraph opens with 'However' or 'Yet', tag it as 'turn' — inference questions concentrate on these paragraphs and you can go there first.
Count the questions before you start reading. Ten questions on 700 words justifies a careful 4-minute read; five questions on 700 words does not, and you should skim harder and lean on tags.
traps: Spending 12 or more minutes on one RC set and then rushing 25 other questions. The marks lost elsewhere always exceed the marks gained here.
Treating a Mains long passage like a Prelims one and reading the question stems first — you end up reading the passage twice, which is the one thing you cannot afford.
Guessing the third statement in a three-statement question after verifying two. With 0.25 negative marking, that guess loses more often than it wins; verify all three or leave the question.

Inference options that are true of the world and consistent with the passage but not derivable from it. At Mains these are written more carefully than at Prelims and are correspondingly harder to reject.

Skipping the whole set because the passage looks long. At Mains, RC is 13 of 40 marks, and long passages are usually MORE structured than Prelims ones. Skipping RC caps your English score at roughly 27 out of 40.
Not writing the paragraph tags down because 'I'll remember'. Under a 35-minute clock with 40 questions you will not remember, and the whole technique collapses.
Answering a tone question from the topic rather than the author's language, which is easier to do in a long passage because there is more topic to be distracted by.
e-rc-long.timeTarget: 8 to 10 minutes per 8-10 question long set, i.e. 55-65 seconds per question. Reading a 700-word passage with tags: 4 minutes. Vocabulary sub-question: 25 seconds. Detail with tags: 35-40 seconds. Inference: 60 seconds. Multi-statement: 75-90 seconds.
e-rc-long.masteryCheck: On a 700-word Mains-level passage with 10 questions you finish in under 9.5 minutes with 8 or more correct, having written a tag beside every paragraph and read the passage exactly once. Confirm across three different passages before treating it as reliable.
questionPatterns: One 600-800 word passage with 8-10 questions, usually two such sets in a Mains English paper.
Central idea / most appropriate title.
3-4 detail questions distributed across paragraphs in passage order.
2-3 inference questions, at least one clustered around a contrast connector.
Tone or author's attitude.
2-3 vocabulary questions on highlighted words, often testing a secondary meaning.
Multi-statement 'which of the following is/are true' with options like 'Only I and III'.
Occasionally: 'which of the following would weaken the author's argument', or a sentence-replacement question on a highlighted portion.
Themes in recent Mains papers have included science and technology, geography and environment, and economics.
e-rc-long.searchQuery: IBPS clerk mains reading comprehension long passage practice set with solutions inference statement based
e-rc-long.aiPrompt: Act as an IBPS Clerk MAINS paper-setter. Write ONE original 700-word passage in five clearly separated paragraphs, in the register of a long-form Indian newspaper analysis piece, on a science, environment or economic-policy theme. Structure: P1 context, P2 the problem, P3 institutional response, P4 critique of that response, P5 the author's conclusion. Highlight three words in bold, choosing words whose SECONDARY meaning is used in context. Then write 10 IBPS-format questions with five options each: 1 title, 4 detail placed in passage order, 2 inference (one built on a 'However' sentence), 1 tone, 2 vocabulary on the bold words. Include one three-statement question (I, II, III) with options like 'Only I and III'. Then give an answer key that states, for each answer, WHICH PARAGRAPH it came from and quotes the justifying line, plus a one-line reason each wrong option fails. Finally, give a suggested five-word paragraph tag for each of the five paragraphs so I can compare against my own tagging. Do not reveal answers before the key.
e-rc-long.bookRef: S.P. Bakshi, 'Objective General English' (Arihant), Part C — Objective Comprehension, for the question-type grounding. Beyond that, Mains RC is built on previous-year Mains papers and long-form editorial reading, not on a textbook chapter.
e-rc-long.websiteRef: PracticeMock (practicemock.com) Mains-level RC sets; Bankersadda (bankersadda.com); Oliveboard (oliveboard.in) Mains mock series; Testbook (testbook.com) previous-year Mains papers; SmartKeeda Testzone. For reading length-stamina: The Hindu 'Sunday Magazine' and long-form Indian Express pieces.
e-rc-long.weightageNote: About 13 of 40 Mains English questions — roughly a third of a section that directly decides merit, since IBPS Clerk has no interview. Historical Mains RC counts: 10-12 (2023), 12-13 (2022), 10-12 (2021), 11 (2020). This is the single largest block of marks in Mains English.
e-rc-long.blockPlan: 15m: take any 700-word editorial and practise ONLY tagging — read it and write a 3-word label per paragraph, then check whether your tags would let you find five specific facts quickly. No questions, just tagging. 20m untimed: one full 10-question long set with tags, writing the source paragraph beside every answer. 20m timed: one long set with a hard 9-minute stop; whatever is unanswered at 9 minutes stays unanswered, so you feel the cap. 5m: log whether misses were time losses or comprehension losses — at Mains these need opposite fixes.

e-rc-multi.whatItIs: The Mains variant where instead of one long passage you get two or three shorter passages of 200-350 words, each with 3-5 questions. The economics are completely different from a long set, and applying long-passage habits here loses time.
e-rc-multi.coreMethod:
1. UNDERSTAND WHY THE STRATEGY FLIPS. In a short set you pay a fresh comprehension start-up cost for every passage, so the reading-to-question ratio is worse. But each passage is small enough to hold entirely in working memory. Both facts push you toward question-first and away from tagging.
2. QUESTION-FIRST DOES PAY HERE — the opposite of the long-passage rule. For a 300-word passage with 4 questions: read the 4 stems (15 seconds), read the passage once (90-110 seconds), then answer. The stems are cheap to read and tell you exactly what to hold on to.
3. TRIAGE ACROSS SETS BEFORE STARTING. Spend 20 seconds looking at all the short passages and begin with the one whose TOPIC YOU KNOW BEST. There is no requirement to do them in printed order, and topic familiarity is worth 60-90 seconds per set. This is free time and almost nobody takes it.
4. PER-SET BUDGET: 15 seconds on stems + 90-110 seconds reading + 35 seconds per question. A 4-question set is 4 minutes; a 3-question set is 3.2 minutes. Enforce the cap per set, not across the block, or one bad passage silently eats the others.
5. DO NOT SKIM SHORT PASSAGES. Short passages have almost no redundancy — nearly every sentence carries an answer. Read them at a slightly SLOWER pace than a long passage. Skimming only works when there is filler to skip, and here there is none.
6. EXPECT DETAIL TO DOMINATE. Theme and tone questions need length to be fair, so short sets typically run 2-3 detail + 1 vocabulary + at most 1 inference. Attack detail-first here rather than vocabulary-first.
7. COMPARATIVE VARIANTS ('Passage A argues X, Passage B argues Y — identify a point of disagreement'): write the two claims in two columns on the rough sheet BEFORE looking at options, then match. Trying to hold both claims in your head while reading five options is where this variant is lost.
8. DO NOT TAG. Paragraph tagging is a long-passage tool. Using it on a 250-word passage wastes 20 seconds for no retrieval benefit.
tricks: Triage by topic familiarity before you start — this is the highest-return 20 seconds in the whole Mains English paper and costs you nothing.
In a short passage the central idea is almost always in the FIRST or LAST sentence. If a theme question appears, check those two sentences before reading anything else.
If two short sets share a theme (both on climate, both on technology), do them back to back. The vocabulary is already loaded and the second set runs 30-40 seconds faster.

Judge attempt-worthiness by question type, not passage length. A 3-question set that is all detail is worth attempting; a 3-question set with 2 inference plus 1 tone has a reading cost that is not repaid if time is tight.

Read the stems, then read the passage with those stems consciously in mind — in a 250-word passage you will usually recognise the answer sentence as you pass it, and can mark it, answering three questions almost without a second pass.

When two short passages are given as a linked pair (Passage A and Passage B), read BOTH stems before reading either passage. Some questions require both, and discovering that after reading only A costs you a re-read.
traps: Reading all the passages first and then answering all the questions. You will have forgotten passage 1 by the time you finish passage 3, and you will re-read — which destroys the format's only advantage.
Applying long-passage skimming to a short passage. Short Mains passages are dense; skim one and you will miss the single sentence a detail question was built on.
Assuming shorter means easier. Short Mains passages are frequently more abstract and more compressed than long ones — the compression is exactly what makes them hard.
Losing the running clock across three sets because you are only watching the section timer. Set and enforce a per-set cap.
Building a mental map or tags for a 250-word passage. It is wasted effort that feels productive.
Doing the sets in printed order out of habit and hitting the hardest topic first while you still have 30 minutes of paper left.
In comparative A/B variants, answering about passage A when the stem asked about passage B. Circle the letter in the stem before reading options.

e-error-1.whatItIs: The foundational format: a sentence split into 3-5 labelled parts, with one part containing a grammatical error and a final option reading 'No error'. About 4-5 questions in Prelims and 5-6 in Mains, and the format that all your grammar study cashes out into.
e-error-1.coreMethod:
1. READ THE SENTENCE ONCE AT NORMAL SPEED WITHOUT HUNTING. Most planted errors sound wrong on a natural read. Hunting rule-by-rule from the first word is slower than reading and then hunting. The scan below is what you do when nothing jumped out.
2. THE 7-POINT SCAN, run in this order because it matches IBPS's actual error frequency:
   (1) VERB AGREEMENT — find the main verb, strip modifiers, check number. Roughly 30% of errors.
   (2) TENSE AND VERB FORM — check time markers; check the participle after each auxiliary (has/have/had + V3, is/are/was/were + V-ing or V3, did/does + V1, modal + V1). ~20%.
   (3) PREPOSITION — check each preposition against its governing verb, adjective or noun. ~15%.
   (4) ARTICLE AND DETERMINER — every singular countable noun needs one; a/an by sound; 'the' with superlatives. ~10%.
   (5) PRONOUN — case after prepositions, agreement with antecedent. ~10%.
   (6) ADJECTIVE/ADVERB — degree errors, -ly after linking verbs, misplaced 'only'. ~8%.
   (7) CONJUNCTION AND PARALLELISM — correlative partners, parallel structure, word order. ~7%.
3. If nothing trips across all seven, choose 'No error'. At Clerk level this is genuinely the correct answer roughly one time in six to eight — it is not a decoy.
4. THE GUESSING RULE (learn this number, it governs the whole section). With five options and 0.25 negative marking: guessing blind is expected value ZERO; eliminating one option gives +0.06; eliminating two gives +0.17; eliminating three gives +0.375. So: NEVER guess with four or five options live; ALWAYS guess once you are down to three or fewer. Convert hesitation into this rule and stop deliberating.
5. Hard cap of 30-35 seconds. If you cannot place the error in that time, apply the guessing rule and move.
tricks: Check the SHORT parts first. Error-detection sentences are split unevenly, and a two-or-three-word part containing a preposition, an article or a comparative is a favourite hiding place that takes three seconds to clear.
If two parts both look wrong, choose the one containing the VERB. IBPS builds the majority of its items around verbs, and agreement/tense errors outnumber everything else roughly two to one.

Memorise these as SHAPES, not rules — you will spot them without parsing: 'discuss about', 'prefer than', 'senior than', 'one of the + singular noun', 'more better', 'informations', 'return back', 'revert back', 'repeat again', 'cope up with', 'comprises of', 'married with', 'since two years', 'each of the boys are', 'the number of ... are', 'hardly ... than', 'lest ... not', 'order for'. Each is a two-second recognition and together they cover a large share of real items.
Never change the MEANING to fix the sentence. If your correction alters what the sentence says, it is not the intended error and you are on the wrong track — restart the scan.
When the error involves agreement across two parts, the answer is the part containing the VERB, not the part containing the subject. Aspirants regularly mark the right error in the wrong part.
Before marking 'No error', do one deliberate check of the prepositions and articles only. These are the errors that survive a natural read, because Indian English normalises them.
traps: Marking a part wrong because it sounds unusual but is grammatically correct — especially inversion after 'Never', 'Seldom', 'Hardly', 'Not only' at the start of a sentence.
Choosing 'No error' as a safety option when you are unsure. If you feel unsure you probably half-saw something; a blind 'No error' is just a one-in-five guess worth exactly zero.

Indian-English usages that read as completely normal: 'revert back to me', 'discuss about the matter', 'cope up with the pressure', 'order for a book', 'good in English' (should be good AT), 'different than' (should be different FROM), 'sit in the table'. These are the errors you will most often read straight past.

Fixating on vocabulary or word choice. Error Detection tests GRAMMAR. If the only thing odd about a part is that a word is unusual, that is almost certainly not the error — word choice is tested separately as word usage and word swap.
Reading only inside part boundaries and never across them. Agreement, correlatives and sequence-of-tense errors span two parts by design.
Spending 60 seconds on one error-detection question. It is worth exactly one mark, the same as a 20-second one, and in a 20-minute sectional paper that is a two-question loss.
Assuming that a long, complex-looking part is more likely to hold the error. Setters frequently hide the fault in the shortest part precisely because candidates skim it.
e-error-1.timeTarget: 30-35 seconds per question in Prelims. A 5-question error-detection set should be finished in under 3 minutes — this block is where you bank early marks.
e-error-1.masteryCheck: You solve 20 single-error sentences in 10 minutes with 17 or more correct, AND for every one you got right you can name the specific rule violated. Naming the rule is the real test — recognising an error you cannot explain does not transfer to new sentences.

Sentence split into three parts with a fourth option 'No error'.
Errors concentrated on subject-verb agreement, tense, prepositions and articles, in that frequency order.

e-error-2.whatItIs: The harder rule set that basic error detection does not cover: parallelism, correlative conjunction pairs, redundancy, misplaced and dangling modifiers, the subjunctive, question tags and word order. These are the items that separate a 15 from a 22 in the English section.
e-error-2.coreMethod:
1. PARALLELISM. Items joined by and/or/but, and everything following a correlative pair, must share grammatical form. 'She likes reading, writing and to paint' -> 'painting'. Structural rule for correlatives: what follows 'not only' and what follows 'but also' must be structurally identical. 'He not only sings but also dances' is right; 'He not only sings but also he dances' is wrong.
2. CORRELATIVE PAIRS — memorise the exact partners; a wrong partner IS the error:
   not only ... but also (never plain 'but')
   either ... or / neither ... nor (never 'or' after neither)
   both ... and (never 'as well as' after both)
   no sooner ... than (never 'when')
   hardly / scarcely / barely ... when or before (never 'than')
   such ... that / so ... that / so ... as (in negatives)
   lest ... should (never with 'not' — 'lest he should fall', not 'lest he should not fall')
   although / though ... yet (never 'but')
   as ... as (affirmative) / so ... as (negative)
   the same ... as / such ... as
   unless and until never take a second negative ('unless you do not come' is wrong)
   since / because / as never pair with 'therefore' or 'so' in the same sentence
3. REDUNDANCY. Learn these as phrases: return back, revert back, repeat again, reverse back, join together, mutual cooperation, free gift, new innovation, past history, final conclusion, close proximity, advance planning, cope up with, discuss about, sufficient enough, more preferable, most unique, ascend up, descend down, two twins, complete monopoly, end result, basic fundamentals, small in size, my personal opinion.
4. MISPLACED AND DANGLING MODIFIERS. An introductory participial phrase must attach to the subject that immediately follows it. 'Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful' — the trees were not walking. Check the subject right after the comma.
5. SUBJUNCTIVE. After insist, demand, suggest, recommend, propose, order, request, urge, and after 'it is essential/important/necessary/imperative that' — use bare V1: 'He insisted that she GO' (not goes, not went). Also 'wish', 'as if', 'as though', 'it is high time', 'suppose' take V2 or 'were'.
6. QUESTION TAGS (occasional). Opposite polarity, matching auxiliary and subject. 'Let's go, shall we?' 'I am right, aren't I?' Imperative takes 'will you?'
7. WORD ORDER. 'enough' follows the adjective it modifies; adverbs of frequency sit before the main verb but after 'be'; inversion is required after a negative opener ('Never have I seen', 'Seldom does he come', 'Not only did he arrive late...').
tricks: If the sentence contains not only / either / neither / no sooner / hardly / scarcely / lest / although / unless / as...as — go STRAIGHT to the partner word and check it. In sentences containing these, the pair itself is the error roughly 70% of the time. Ten seconds, no full read required.

Scan for lists joined by 'and' and check the SHAPE of the items, not their meaning. If one item is a gerund, one an infinitive and one a plain noun, that is the error. Parallelism is visually detectable once you look at form.
Learn the redundancy list as phrases, not as a rule. 'Return back', 'cope up with', 'sufficient enough' register in two seconds each with no parsing, and at least one usually appears per paper.

After suggest / insist / demand / recommend / propose / essential that, the next verb must be bare V1. Any -s ending or past form there is the error. This is a favourite Mains item and it is entirely mechanical.
'Lest ... should not' — the 'not' is the error, always. Instantly recognisable shape.

If a sentence opens with a comma-separated -ing phrase, look only at the subject after the comma. Mismatch means a dangling modifier, and the error is in the part after the comma, not in the phrase itself.
traps: Marking inversion as wrong. 'Never had I seen such a sight' and 'Seldom does she complain' are both correct, and both look wrong at speed.
'Enter into' is not always redundant — 'enter into an agreement/contract/discussion/negotiation' is correct English. Only 'enter into the room' is wrong.
Over-applying the subjunctive. The bare-V1 rule applies only to 'that'-clauses. 'He suggested going early' is perfectly correct.
'Each and every' is a redundancy in strict grammar but is idiomatic enough that IBPS rarely keys it — do not choose it if a cleaner error exists in the sentence.
Correcting a parallelism issue that is not there because you did not recognise a form — two gerunds where one carries a long modifier still count as parallel.
Reading straight past a redundancy because it sounds natural in Indian English: 'revert back to me', 'discuss about the matter', 'repeat it again'.
Assuming 'not only ... but' without 'also' is always an error. Modern usage permits it; only mark it if the part boundaries make the correlative the clear focus of the item.
e-error-2.timeTarget: 35-40 seconds per question — genuinely slower than basic error detection because the rule set is larger and less visually obvious. Correlative-pair and redundancy items should still resolve in under 15 seconds once the lists are memorised.
e-error-2.masteryCheck: Given 15 sentences each containing exactly one error drawn from parallelism, correlatives, redundancy, dangling modifiers or the subjunctive, you score 13 or more AND correctly name which of those five categories each error belonged to.

e-error-double.whatItIs: A sentence split into 4-5 parts where TWO parts contain errors and the options are combinations ('A and C', 'B and D', 'Only C', 'All parts are correct'). Also appears inverted as 'which of the following parts is/are grammatically correct'. Same one mark, roughly double the time — which makes selection more important than technique here.
e-error-double.coreMethod:
1. DECIDE WHETHER TO ATTEMPT AT ALL. This format pays the same one mark as a 30-second single-error question but costs 50-60 seconds and requires you to be right about two things instead of one. In Prelims it belongs near the end of your attempt order; in Mains it is worth doing but not first.
2. DO NOT HUNT FOR TWO ERRORS. Evaluate each part INDEPENDENTLY and mark it correct / incorrect / unsure. Then read the options and match. Hunting for 'the second error' after finding the first is how you manufacture false positives — you start inventing faults to satisfy the question.
3. WORK PART BY PART IN ORDER, giving each part a maximum of 8 seconds. For each part ask only four things: (i) is there a verb — check agreement and form; (ii) is there a preposition — check the collocation; (iii) is there an article or determiner — check necessity and a/an; (iv) is there a comparative or correlative — check the partner. Nothing else fits in 8 seconds.
4. WRITE YOUR JUDGEMENTS DOWN: A✓ B✗ C? D✓ on the rough sheet. Mental tracking fails under clock pressure and you will re-check a part you already cleared.
5. USE THE OPTIONS AS A CONSTRAINT, NOT A STARTING POINT. Once you are confident about ONE part, eliminate every option that contradicts it. Two confident judgements often uniquely determine the answer even when you are unsure about the remaining parts. This is the real time-saver in this format.
6. FOR THE INVERTED VERSION ('which parts are grammatically CORRECT'), use the identical procedure and invert only at the matching step. Do not translate the question in your head while solving — that is what causes reversal errors.
7. TAKE 'ALL PARTS ARE CORRECT' SERIOUSLY. In double-error sets this option is keyed more often than candidates expect, precisely because they assume the question guarantees two errors.
8. SKIP RULE: at 60 seconds, if you have one confident error and no option isolates it, apply the guessing rule (guess at three or fewer live options, otherwise leave) and move on.
tricks: Anchor on the part you are MOST sure about and eliminate from there. If you are certain part B is wrong, every option not containing B disappears — in a five-option set that typically leaves two, which is a +0.375 expected-value guess and worth taking.
Do the SHORT parts first. They resolve fastest and give you the anchor you need for elimination, which changes the whole economics of the question.

If you find one error and no second candidate after one full pass, re-check the ARTICLES and PREPOSITIONS in every part. Paper-setters routinely pair one structural error with one small-word error, and the small-word one is what survives a first pass.
If two apparent errors sit in adjacent parts and both involve the same verb phrase, it is usually ONE error split across a part boundary. Recount before choosing a two-error option.

Read the instruction line for the exact number of errors. Some variants say 'two parts', some say 'one or more parts'. The second kind allows a single-error answer and candidates lose marks by refusing to select one.
Note your part judgements as symbols on the rough sheet. The five seconds this costs is repaid the moment you look at the options, because you match instead of re-reading.
traps: Manufacturing a second error because the question implies there are two. If the stem guarantees two and you can only find one, the one you found may be the wrong one — re-examine it rather than inventing a partner.
Marking a part wrong for style rather than grammar. Clunky is not incorrect.
Losing track of which parts you have cleared and re-reading them. This is the single largest time leak in this format.
Reading the options first and then trying to confirm a combination. This biases you into seeing errors that are not there, and it is exactly what the option-writers count on.
Spending 90 seconds for one mark. In Prelims that is three single-error questions forgone.
Assuming 'All parts are correct' is a trap option. It is a genuine key often enough to take seriously.
In the inverted 'which parts are correct' version, answering with the incorrect parts because you solved on autopilot. Circle the word 'correct' or 'incorrect' in the instruction before you begin.

e-error-mains.whatItIs: Error detection as it appears in the Mains paper: longer sentences (25-40 words), subtler errors, and rotating instruction formats including 'find the grammatically correct sentence among five'. Mains English is 40 marks that decide merit directly, and there is no interview to recover from.
e-error-mains.coreMethod:
1. READ THE INSTRUCTION LINE AND CIRCLE THE KEY WORD. Mains rotates between at least four instruction types, and each requires the opposite mental operation:
   (a) 'Which part contains an error?'
   (b) 'Which part has NO error?'
   (c) 'Which of the following sentences is grammatically CORRECT?' (five full sentences)
   (d) 'Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?'
   Misreading the instruction is the most avoidable loss in Mains English and it happens to good candidates under clock pressure.
2. FOR THE FIVE-FULL-SENTENCES FORMAT — do NOT read them as five sentences. The five options are usually variations of the SAME content differing in only two or three specific spots. Scan across the options to locate the differing spots, then judge only those. This converts five 30-word reads into three 3-word decisions. After RC paragraph tagging, this is the highest-value technique in Mains English.
3. RUN THE STANDARD 7-POINT SCAN (agreement, tense/verb form, preposition, article, pronoun, adjective/adverb, conjunction) and then add the Mains-only layer: subjunctive after suggest/demand/insist/essential that; parallelism across long lists; dangling modifiers; sequence of tenses across three clauses; articles before abstract and uncountable nouns; 'one of the + plural + who + plural verb'; comma splices.
4. IN LONG SENTENCES, FIND THE MAIN CLAUSE FIRST. Identify the main subject and main verb and check them. Then check each subordinate clause separately. Mains sentences hide the error in the main clause while burying it under subordinate detail.
5. UNDERLINE THE MAIN VERB the moment you find it. In a 35-word sentence, losing track of the main verb is how you burn 30 seconds re-reading.
6. BUDGET 45-55 seconds. Mains gives 52.5 seconds per question overall, and error detection deserves roughly that. If the sentence needs a third read, apply the guessing rule and move.
7. APPLY THE ELIMINATION-COUNT RULE STRICTLY at Mains, because these marks decide the merit list: attempt if you can eliminate two or more options; leave it otherwise.
tricks: The compare-the-differing-spots technique for five-full-sentence options. Practise it deliberately on 30 items — it is worth 60 or more seconds per question and most candidates never discover it.
In a 35-word sentence, the error is more often in the FIRST or the LAST clause than in the middle. Setters place it where you read fastest (the opening) or where attention drops (the end).

Any sentence containing a semicolon or a '; however,' construction: check whether both sides are independent clauses. Comma splices and connector misuse are tested at Mains and never at Prelims, so this check is nearly free information.

If the sentence contains a reporting verb (said, told, claimed, argued, stated) plus 'that', check two things only: tense sequence, and whether the reported content is a universal truth that should stay present.
At Mains, 'No error' is a genuine key more often than at Prelims. Do not treat it as a decoy — treating it as one costs real marks in a section that decides your rank.

When two usages in a sentence are both defensible in modern English (different from/than, none is/are, each other/one another, whether/if), that part is almost certainly NOT the intended error. Move past it immediately rather than deliberating.
traps: Misreading 'correct' as 'incorrect' in the instruction. Circle the key word before reading option A — this single habit prevents the most expensive Mains English error.
Applying a Prelims-speed 30-second cap to a 40-word Mains sentence and mis-marking. Mains gives you more time per question; use it here rather than rushing and then having spare time at the end.
Assuming complexity implies error. Long, correct sentences are deliberately used as decoys in the five-sentence format.
Being caught by two acceptable usages and deliberating for 40 seconds over a part that was never the intended answer.
Treating 'No error' as unavailable at Mains because you have been trained on Prelims papers where you rarely selected it.
Reading all five full sentences end to end in the (c)/(d) format instead of comparing differing spots — this is a two-minute question if done wrong and a 40-second question if done right.
Neglecting the subjunctive and dangling-modifier rules because they rarely appear at Prelims. At Mains they appear regularly and are the difference between 5/6 and 3/6 on this block.

e-improvement.whatItIs: A phrase in a sentence is underlined or bolded and you choose the best replacement, with 'No improvement required' as a live option. Also called phrase replacement. It tests the same grammar as error detection but requires you to produce the correction, not just locate the fault.
e-improvement.coreMethod:
1. READ THE WHOLE SENTENCE, not just the underlined part. The fault is frequently a mismatch between the underlined portion and something OUTSIDE it — the subject (for agreement), a time marker (for tense), or a correlative partner.
2. PREDICT THE CORRECTION BEFORE LOOKING AT THE OPTIONS. Say the fixed version in your head, then find the option closest to it. This is the core discipline of the question type. Reading the options first makes all five sound plausible and roughly doubles your time.
3. DIAGNOSE THE CATEGORY, in IBPS frequency order: verb form or tense -> preposition -> correlative or conjunction -> parallelism -> redundancy -> pronoun case -> article -> word order -> idiom. Naming the category tells you what to look for in the options.
4. ELIMINATE MEANING-CHANGERS. Options that alter what the sentence says are wrong even when they are grammatically perfect. Improvement questions test grammar and idiom, not rewriting. Cross out anything that adds or removes information.
5. PREFER THE SHORTEST GRAMMATICALLY CORRECT OPTION. Bank answer keys favour concision. Options padded with 'in order to', 'due to the fact that', 'the reason being that', 'on account of the fact' are decoys nearly every time.
6. SUBSTITUTE AND RE-READ. Put your chosen option back into the full sentence and read it once. Five seconds, and it catches the 'right fix, wrong tense' trap that is otherwise invisible.
7. 'NO IMPROVEMENT REQUIRED' is correct roughly one time in six. Choose it only after running the diagnosis — but do choose it when the diagnosis comes back clean.
tricks: Predict-then-match is the whole game. It is the difference between a 30-second solve and a 70-second one, and it is a habit rather than a piece of knowledge — you have to force it for two weeks before it sticks.

Scan the underlined portion for the usual suspects in five seconds: is there a preposition, a verb form, a correlative word, a comparative, or a pronoun? Whichever one is present is what the question is testing. You now know the category before reading a single option.

If the underlined part contains 'being', be immediately suspicious. 'Being' is wrong in the large majority of bank improvement items — 'The work being done by him' -> 'The work done by him'. A one-word signal with a high hit rate.

If the five options differ only in their preposition, you are being tested on a collocation, not on logic. Go straight to the governing verb or adjective and recall the pair; do not reason about meaning.

If there is a time marker OUTSIDE the underlined portion (since, ago, by the time, last year, already), the answer is a tense fix. You can often select it from the options without fully parsing the sentence.

When two options are structurally identical and differ only in formality of a word, choose the more standard and idiomatic one. Bank keys avoid rare vocabulary in improvement questions — the answer is almost never the fanciest option.
traps: Choosing the option that 'sounds better' stylistically instead of the one that fixes the actual grammatical fault. Style is not tested; grammar and idiom are.
Ignoring everything outside the underlined portion — especially the subject, which determines agreement, and time markers, which determine tense.

Picking an option that fixes the identified error but introduces a new one. This is exactly what the substitute-and-re-read step exists to catch, and skipping that step is the most common single cause of loss here.
Being afraid of 'No improvement required'. At Clerk level a meaningful fraction of these genuinely need no change, and candidates who never select it are systematically losing those marks.
Options that are perfectly correct English but change the meaning — swapping 'should' for 'must', 'many' for 'all', 'may' for 'will'. Grammatical correctness is necessary, not sufficient.
Assuming the underlined part must be wrong because it was underlined. The format explicitly allows it to be right.
Reading all five options before forming your own correction, which is the single habit that makes this question type slow.
e-improvement.timeTarget: 25-35 seconds per question. A 5-question improvement set should be done in under 3 minutes. Anything over 45 seconds means you skipped the prediction step and are comparing options against each other instead of against a target.
e-improvement.masteryCheck: You solve 20 improvement questions in 10 minutes with 17 or more correct, AND in at least 15 of the 20 you had predicted the correction in your head before reading the options. questionPatterns: A phrase underlined or bolded within a sentence, five replacement options, with 'No improvement/No correction required' as one option.

Correlative pair fixes: the underlined part contains one half of a not only/either/no sooner pair.
Redundancy removal: the underlined part contains 'return back', 'cope up with', 'sufficient enough'.
'Being' constructions that need to be simplified.
Parallelism fixes in a list.
Word-order fixes, especially misplaced 'only' and 'enough'.
Occasional Mains hybrid where the question asks which of two or three highlighted phrases needs replacement.

e-vocab.whatItIs: Every question type where the answer depends on what a word means in a specific sentence: RC synonyms and antonyms, word usage, word swap, single and double fillers, and misspelt words. Note the framing — IBPS tests words in context, so word-list memorisation transfers poorly and context substitution transfers completely.
e-vocab.coreMethod:
1. STOP LEARNING ISOLATED WORD LISTS. The same word is right in one sentence and wrong in another; the exam tests fit, not recall. The method below is substitution, not memory.
2. RC SYNONYM/ANTONYM: go to the word, read its sentence plus the one before. Determine POLARITY first — is the required word positive, negative or neutral, based on the surrounding language? Eliminate every option with the wrong polarity; this typically kills two or three options in five seconds. Then substitute the survivors into the actual sentence and pick the one that reads naturally.
3. WORD USAGE ('in which sentence(s) is the word used correctly'): check the PART OF SPEECH first. Most wrong sentences misuse the word as the wrong part of speech — a noun used as a verb, an adjective used as an adverb. This resolves about half of these questions without knowing the precise meaning.
4. WORD SWAP (two words must be interchanged): locate the two content words that feel semantically misplaced, then test only SAME-PART-OF-SPEECH pairs — noun with noun, verb with verb, adjective with adjective. Swap them mentally and re-read. If the sentence now expresses a coherent idea, that is the answer. Never test all possible pairs; that is what makes candidates slow here.
5. FILLERS AND DOUBLE FILLERS: fill the blank you are SURE about first and eliminate on that basis alone. Never try to satisfy both blanks simultaneously. Then check connector logic — but/however/although/yet demands a contrast between the two halves; and/moreover/furthermore demands continuation; because/since/as demands cause.
6. MISSPELT WORDS: the exam draws from a small pool. Learn the trouble patterns rather than individual words — double letters (accommodate, occurrence, necessary, embarrass, recommend, occasion, committee, harass, tomorrow, address, aggressive), -ceed/-cede/-sede (only proceed, succeed, exceed take -ceed; supersede is the only -sede), -ance vs -ence (existence, persistence, maintenance, perseverance, independence), and silent-letter words (privilege, definitely, separate, government, environment, February, restaurant, entrepreneur, liaison, questionnaire, rhythm, bureaucracy, conscience).
7. BUILD VOCABULARY FROM WHAT YOU READ. Every unknown word from your daily editorial goes into a notebook WITH THE SENTENCE it appeared in, not with a dictionary definition alone. Twenty words a week from real reading beats a hundred from a list, because contextual fit is the thing being tested.
tricks: Polarity-first elimination is the fastest move in the whole vocabulary area. Decide positive/negative/neutral before you consider precise meaning — it removes two or three options in five seconds with no vocabulary knowledge at all.

Decode unknown words by affix: mal-, mis-, dis-, un-, in-, non-, anti- signal negative; bene-, pro-, eu- signal positive; -ous and -ful signal adjective; -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity signal noun; -ise, -ify, -en signal verb. Enough to place an unknown word's polarity and part of speech in three seconds, which is often enough to answer.

In double fillers, count the options first. If three options share the same FIRST word, the second blank is the discriminator — solve the second blank only, and ignore the first entirely. And vice versa. A pure structural shortcut that saves 20 or more seconds per question.

In word-swap questions, the swapped pair is almost always in DIFFERENT clauses of the sentence, not adjacent to each other. Look across the comma or conjunction first rather than scanning left to right.
If a synonym question's options include two words that are near-synonyms of EACH OTHER, neither is usually the key — the answer key avoids ambiguity. Look at the other three first.

Learn the ~30 confusable pairs that recur in bank papers: affect/effect, principal/principle, complement/compliment, stationary/stationery, adapt/adopt, elicit/illicit, eminent/imminent, moral/morale, council/counsel, cite/site/sight, precede/proceed, accept/except, assure/ensure/insure, discreet/discrete, loose/lose, farther/further, lie/lay, historic/historical, economic/economical, continual/continuous, credible/credulous, ingenious/ingenuous, judicial/judicious, negligent/negligible, official/officious, respectable/respectful/respective, sensible/sensitive. These are pure marks and they repeat across years.
traps: Choosing the dictionary-primary meaning instead of the contextual one. RC synonym questions frequently use a secondary sense of a common word, and the primary meaning is always offered as an option.
Translating the word to Hindi and back to choose an option. The register shifts in translation and you end up picking a word of the wrong formality.

Selecting a word that fits grammatically but carries the wrong connotation: frugal versus stingy, confident versus arrogant, assertive versus aggressive, inexpensive versus cheap. Connotation is what these questions are built on.

In word swap, choosing a pair that makes the sentence grammatical but changes the intended meaning. The correct swap RESTORES the sentence's original logical sense — if your swap produces a sentence that is fine but says something odd, it is wrong.
Memorising lists you never encounter in context. You will recognise the word in the option and still not know whether it fits the sentence, which is exactly what is being tested.
In fillers, committing on the strength of the first word without checking the second. Always verify both before selecting, even when the first word is a perfect fit.
Assuming misspelt-word questions need broad spelling knowledge. They draw from a narrow, repeating pool — learn the pool rather than trying to become a good speller.

e-cloze.whatItIs:
A connected passage of roughly 100-150 words with five to seven numbered blanks. Each blank offers five word choices and you pick the one that fits. Unlike a fill-in-the-blank standalone, the blanks share one context, so an earlier blank constrains a later one and the passage as a whole has a direction.

At Prelims level the options are usually not near-synonyms. A typical item offers one word that fits, one that is grammatically impossible in the slot, one that points the wrong way, and two that are simply from a different semantic field. That means most blanks are decided by a mechanical check rather than by fine vocabulary judgement — which is why this topic is learnable to a high accuracy in a way that pure vocabulary is not.

The passage topics recur: digital payments and UPI, financial inclusion, climate and environment, public health, education access, MSME credit. The vocabulary recycles heavily across shifts, so a modest, targeted word list beats broad vocabulary reading for this specific topic.

What makes cloze economically attractive is the shape of the cost: you pay the reading cost once and it is amortised across five to seven marks. What makes candidates lose it is getting stuck: because the blanks share a passage, one blank you refuse to abandon can eat the budget for the other five.
e-cloze.coreMethod:
1. FIRST READ, OPTIONS COVERED (28-32 seconds). Read the passage end to end treating each blank as a silent gap. Do not glance at the option lists. Your goal is one sentence you could say aloud: what is this passage claiming, and is it positive or negative about it. Cover the options with your hand or the question paper edge if you have to — this is a physical habit worth building, because the pull to peek is strong and peeking destroys the direction read.

2. TAG THE DIRECTION. Write '+' or '-' at the top of the passage. If the passage turns partway (common: two sentences of praise, then 'However'), draw a line at the turn and tag each half.

3. FOR EACH BLANK, NAME THE SLOT BEFORE READING OPTIONS. Say to yourself: noun, or verb, or adjective, or adverb, or connector — and if verb, which form. This takes about three seconds and it is the highest-value three seconds in the topic, because at Prelims level a wrong-part-of-speech option is present in most items and dies instantly.

4. NOW READ THE FIVE OPTIONS AND STRIKE THE IMPOSSIBLE ONES. Kill on: wrong part of speech; wrong verb form or tense against the surrounding clause; singular/plural clash with the following noun; an option that cannot take the preposition already printed after the blank.

5. APPLY THE DIRECTION TAG to whatever survives. If this half of the passage is tagged '-', a positively-charged survivor is out. Watch for local flippers inside the sentence — despite, although, yet, far from, rather than, no longer — which reverse the polarity for that clause only.

6. APPLY THE COLLOCATION CHECK to the last two survivors. Read the three words before and the three words after the blank and ask which survivor actually partners with them: 'display a QR code', 'a pace few can match', 'address a shortfall', 'bridge a gap'. The adjacent noun or verb is the evidence, and this decides most two-way splits in under five seconds.

7. SUBSTITUTE AND READ THE WHOLE SENTENCE back once with your choice in. Not the phrase — the sentence. Agreement and tense problems live at sentence distance.

8. SWEEP THE EASY BLANKS FIRST, then return. Do a pass through all the blanks answering only the ones that fall out in under 15 seconds, then a second pass on the leftovers. By the second pass you have read the passage twice more in effect, and the direction is much sharper, so blanks that felt impossible frequently resolve. This two-pass order is the main reason a well-run cloze set finishes inside budget.

9. PER-BLANK CAP: 20 seconds on the first pass, 25 seconds on the second. If a blank is still open at the second-pass cap, decide by elimination count, not by feel: two or more options eliminated means mark the best survivor, because with three left the expected value is (1/3 x 1) + (2/3 x -0.25) = +0.17 per mark. Fewer than two eliminated means leave it blank — a blind five-way guess is worth exactly (1/5 x 1) + (4/5 x -0.25) = 0, so it adds nothing to your score while it drags your accuracy.

10. DO NOT RE-READ THE PASSAGE A THIRD TIME for a single blank. If two passes plus 25 seconds have not resolved it, more reading will not; the information you need is not in the passage, it is in vocabulary you either have or do not.
tricks: Cover the options physically during the first read. It sounds trivial and it is worth 15-20 seconds across a set, because reading five candidate words per blank while you read the passage means you finish knowing the vocabulary and not the direction — and direction is what settles the polarity blanks.

Two-pass sweep, not linear order. Answering blanks in printed order forces you to solve blank 2 before you have seen the sentence that disambiguates it. Take the free ones first; the passage gets easier as you fill it in.

Name the part of speech before you look at the options. Three seconds of naming kills one or two of the five options outright at Prelims level, and it stops you from comparing meanings between words that were never grammatically eligible.

When two options both fit the meaning, look only at the word touching the blank. 'a sharp ______ in exports' versus 'a sharp ______ of reserves' separates decline from depletion faster than any reasoning about what the passage is saying.

If a preposition is already printed right after the blank, check it first — it is the cheapest elimination available and frequently reduces five options to two before you have thought about meaning at all.

Build a passage-topic word bank rather than a general vocabulary list. Cloze passages recycle a narrow band of themes (UPI and digital payments, financial inclusion, climate, MSME credit, public health), and thirty words per theme with their usual partners will cover more cloze blanks than three hundred general words.
traps: Reading the options during the first pass. It is the default behaviour and it is the main cause of slow cloze sets: you lose the direction read, then have to reconstruct direction blank by blank, which is five times the work.

Solving blanks strictly in printed order. Blank 1 is often the hardest because you have the least context at that point; candidates spend 40 seconds on it, then discover blank 4 would have taken eight.

Missing a mid-passage turn. A 'However' or 'Yet' at the start of a sentence flips the polarity for everything after it, and a candidate carrying the first half's tag through the whole passage will get the last two blanks pointing the wrong way while each individually 'sounds fine'.

Testing the word in a four-word window. The option is chosen to look right locally. Subject-verb agreement across a long subject and tense clash with the neighbouring clause only surface on a full-sentence read.

Ignoring a printed preposition after the blank. 'was ______ to weaker demand' rules out every option that does not take 'to', but candidates read past the preposition because it is small and already printed.

Refusing to abandon one blank. Because the blanks share one passage, over-investing in a hard blank does not just cost that mark — it forces you to rush the remaining four or five, so a single 60-second blank routinely converts a 6/6 set into 3/6.

Treating cloze as a vocabulary test and skipping it if your vocabulary feels weak. At Prelims level the majority of blanks are decided by part of speech, form, preposition or direction — mechanical checks that work regardless of how large your word list is.

questionPatterns: Standard Prelims item with a mechanical kill available: 'India's digital payment system has grown at a pace that few countries can ______.' Options: (a) resist (b) match (c) refuse (d) collect (e) borrow. Answer (b) match — the collocation is 'a pace few can match'; resist, refuse, collect and borrow do not partner with 'pace'.

Part-of-speech / collocation item: 'Small merchants who once dealt only in cash now ______ a QR code at every counter.' Options: (a) display (b) declare (c) donate (d) delete (e) devour. Answer (a) display — 'display a QR code' is the fixed pairing.

Polarity item with a local flipper: 'Although rural account openings rose sharply, the share of accounts that remain active is still ______.' Options: (a) encouraging (b) impressive (c) modest (d) substantial (e) considerable. Answer (c) modest — 'Although' plus 'still' forces the second clause negative, and the other four are all positive or large-magnitude.

Preposition-locked item: 'The slowdown in disbursement has been attributed ______ a shortage of field officers.' Options: (a) with (b) for (c) to (d) on (e) at. Answer (c) to — 'attributed to' is fixed.

Connector blank inside a passage: 'Deposits grew steadily through the year; ______, lending to small businesses contracted for two consecutive quarters.' Options: (a) therefore (b) however (c) moreover (d) likewise (e) accordingly. Answer (b) however — the two clauses run in opposite directions, and the other four are all same-direction connectors.
