e-cloze-replace.whatItIs:
A passage is printed with several words highlighted, numbered or bolded. Nothing is missing. Your job for each highlighted word is to decide whether it is contextually and grammatically correct as printed, or whether it should be swapped for one of the alternatives offered. The fifth option is almost always some version of 'No correction required' / 'No replacement required', and that option is a live answer, not a decoy.

Banks label this family in several ways and the labels drift between shifts: 'Inappropriate Word in Passage', 'Word Replacement', 'Misspelt or Inappropriate Word', 'Correct/Incorrect Sentences'. Structurally they are one skill with two settings — passage-level (a connected paragraph with 5-7 highlighted words) and sentence-level (independent sentences, one highlighted word each). The passage-level version is harder because a word can be individually fine and still wrong for the paragraph's direction.

The cognitive demand is the inverse of blank-type cloze. In blank cloze you generate a fit for an empty slot; here a plausible word is already sitting in the slot and your default reading will accept it. The skill is manufactured suspicion applied by rule, and it is the reason this topic is genuinely hard: reading fluently is what makes you miss the error.

The errors planted are a small, finite, learnable set: (i) confusable pairs (affect/effect, principal/principle, comprise/compose, elicit/illicit, complement/compliment); (ii) transitivity and form errors (rise for raise, lie for lay, lose for loose); (iii) wrong preposition inside a fixed phrase; (iv) polarity reversal — a word whose meaning is correct English but points against the paragraph; (v) collocation break — the word is right in meaning and wrong in partner ('do a mistake', 'severe rain'); (vi) part-of-speech slip (an adjective where the slot needs an adverb).
e-cloze-replace.coreMethod:
1. READ THE PASSAGE ONCE STRAIGHT THROUGH (40-45 seconds for a 150-200 word passage), ignoring the highlights entirely. You need the paragraph's direction before you can judge any single word, and a highlighted word that is polarity-wrong is invisible until you know which way the argument runs. Mark each paragraph '+' or '-' in the margin.

2. TAKE THE HIGHLIGHTED WORDS ONE AT A TIME, IN ORDER, and for each one read the FULL sentence it sits in — not the phrase. Most planted errors only become visible at sentence length, because the error is agreement, tense, or a preposition four words away.

3. RUN THE FIVE-CHECK SWEEP on the printed word, in this fixed order, stopping the moment one check fails. (i) PART OF SPEECH: does the slot want a noun, verb, adjective or adverb, and is the printed word that? (ii) FORM: correct tense, correct number, correct participle, and — if the word is a verb — is it transitive or intransitive to match what actually follows it? (iii) PREPOSITION: if a preposition is printed nearby, does this word take that one? (iv) COLLOCATION: does this word actually pair with the noun or verb it is attached to in edited English? (v) POLARITY: does its direction agree with the '+' or '-' you marked in step 1, and with any despite / although / yet in the sentence? A word that clears all five is correct as printed.

4. ONLY NOW READ THE FIVE OPTIONS. Reading options first is what makes this topic slow: an option list will make you doubt a perfectly good word and you will burn 20 seconds relitigating a decision you had already made correctly. Decide first, then look.

5. IF YOUR SWEEP FOUND THE PRINTED WORD SOUND, look for 'No correction required' among the five and mark it. Do not overrule your own sweep because the option list looks tempting. This is the single most common way marks are thrown away in this topic — candidates who correctly judged the word then talked themselves into a replacement.

6. IF YOUR SWEEP FAILED THE PRINTED WORD, you already know WHICH check failed, so use that check as the filter on the four replacements. Failed on transitivity: keep only options that take an object. Failed on preposition: keep only options that take the printed preposition. Failed on polarity: keep only options pointing the right way. This turns a five-way comparison into a one-rule lookup, which is where the time saving in this topic actually comes from.

7. SUBSTITUTE AND READ THE WHOLE SENTENCE BACK once with your chosen replacement in place. Replacement-type distractors are built to fix the local phrase and break something else in the sentence — commonly the tense of a following clause or agreement with a distant subject.

8. PASSAGE-LEVEL COHERENCE PASS (about 15 seconds, only on the passage version). Read your final set of choices as a paragraph. Two highlighted words that now say the same thing, or a pair that now contradict, means one of them is wrong. This pass catches the polarity item you accepted at sentence level.

9. STOPPING RULE: 35 seconds per highlighted word. At the cap, if you have eliminated two or more options, mark the best survivor — three remaining options against 0.25 negative gives expected value (1/3 x 1) + (2/3 x -0.25) = +0.17. If you have eliminated fewer than two, leave it blank: a blind five-way guess is worth exactly (1/5 x 1) + (4/5 x -0.25) = 0 and costs you accuracy for no expected gain.
tricks: Judge the printed word BEFORE you look at the options, every single time. This is the whole topic in one habit: it converts each item from a five-way comparison into a yes/no verdict plus a filtered lookup, and it is worth roughly 10-12 seconds per item across a 7-item set.

Learn the confusable-pair list as pairs, not as words. affect/effect, principal/principle, comprise/compose, elicit/illicit, complement/compliment, adverse/averse, eminent/imminent, stationary/stationery, altogether/all together, farther/further. Recognising that a printed word HAS a confusable twin is itself the alarm — you then only have to decide which twin the sentence wants.

When the highlighted word is a verb, check transitivity first rather than meaning. rise/raise, lie/lay, fall/fell, sit/set — whether an object follows the gap decides these in about three seconds, whereas reasoning about meaning can take twenty and still not decide.

Treat 'No correction required' as roughly as likely as any other option and let your sweep decide it. Never adopt a policy about how often it appears — with 0.25 negative marking, any policy that substitutes for the five-check sweep will cost you marks the moment the paper's mix differs from the mix you assumed.

On the passage version, do the highlighted words in printed order rather than easiest-first. The paragraph's argument is built cumulatively, so a later word's polarity often depends on how you read an earlier one; jumping around forces you to re-establish direction repeatedly.

If two replacement options both survive your filter, put each into the sentence and read to the END of the following sentence. Replacement distractors typically break the link to the next sentence rather than the current one.
traps: Reading the options first. The option list is engineered to make a correct printed word look doubtful; once you have read five alternatives you can no longer judge the original cleanly, and you will spend an extra 15-20 seconds and often land on a replacement you did not need.

Rejecting 'No correction required' on principle, or reaching for it whenever you are unsure. Both are policies rather than checks. The first loses every genuinely-correct item; the second turns every hard item into a bet.

Judging the highlighted word from the phrase around it. 'A severe increase in rainfall' looks fine in four words; the collocation break ('severe' pairs with damage, shortage, drought — not with increase) is only obvious once you read the whole sentence.

Accepting a word that is correct English but points the wrong way for the paragraph. This is the specific error the passage-level format exists to test, and it is undetectable at sentence level — which is why the step-1 direction read and the step-8 coherence pass are not optional.

Fixing the local phrase and breaking the sentence. A replacement that repairs the preposition but leaves the verb disagreeing with a distant subject is the standard trap; the substitute-and-read-back step is what catches it.

Treating the sentence-level version and the passage-level version as the same difficulty and budgeting the same time. The passage version carries a coherence pass the sentence version does not, and needs roughly a third more time per item.

Assuming today's paper will use the label you practised. The same skill has appeared as Inappropriate Word in Passage, Word Replacement, Misspelt Word and Correct/Incorrect Sentences; candidates who trained on one label lose 15-20 seconds re-orienting when another appears.

questionPatterns: Passage-level: 'In the passage below, some words are highlighted. For each, choose the option that should replace it. If the highlighted word is correct as printed, choose No correction required.' Item: '…the new policy is expected to RISE employment across the textile clusters…' Options: (a) raise (b) arise (c) rouse (d) No correction required (e) rinse. Answer (a) raise — the slot takes a direct object ('employment'), and rise and arise are intransitive.

Confusable pair with the printed word correct: 'Rising input costs have severely AFFECTED the margins of small exporters.' Options: (a) effected (b) infected (c) No correction required (d) inflicted (e) reflected. Answer (c) — 'affect' as the verb meaning 'influence' is correct here; 'effected' would mean 'brought about', which the sentence does not.

Preposition lock: 'The shortfall in advance tax collections has been attributed ON weaker festive demand.' Options: (a) to (b) for (c) with (d) No correction required (e) from. Answer (a) to — attributed takes 'to'; note this variant highlights the preposition itself rather than the content word.

Polarity item, passage-level: in a paragraph arguing that a scheme has under-delivered — '…which is why the rollout has been widely COMMENDED by rural credit officers.' Options: (a) criticised (b) celebrated (c) endorsed (d) applauded (e) No correction required. Answer (a) criticised — commended, celebrated, endorsed and applauded are all positive and clash with the paragraph's direction; only the polarity check finds this, since the sentence is flawless in isolation.

Sentence-level variant: 'Neither the branch manager nor the clerks WAS informed of the revised guideline.' Options: (a) were (b) has been (c) is (d) No correction required (e) have. Answer (a) were — the proximity rule makes the verb agree with the nearer subject 'clerks'.

e-cloze-mains.whatItIs:
A 150-220 word passage with seven numbered gaps, each offering five word choices. It is the same skeleton as the Prelims cloze but three things change and each one breaks a Prelims habit.

First, the options stop being wrong-versus-right and become near-synonyms. Where Prelims offers 'match / refuse / borrow / collect / resist', Mains offers 'curb / stem / halt / quell / restrain' — five words that all mean roughly 'stop', separated only by what they are allowed to combine with. Meaning alone will not choose between them.

Second, some gaps are structural rather than lexical: the blank wants a connector (whereas, thereby, albeit, notwithstanding) or a preposition inside a fixed phrase, and the answer is decided by the syntax on either side rather than by sense.

Third, the passage is argumentative — RBI policy, fiscal consolidation, climate finance, labour formalisation — so gaps carry direction. A word that is right in dictionary meaning but wrong in polarity (positive where the clause needs negative) is the standard distractor.

A warning about a technique you may have been taught: do not select by 'register', i.e. do not reason that the most formal or most editorial-sounding of the five words is the intended one. In a genuine Mains set all five options are drawn from the same register precisely so that this shortcut fails, and treating formality as evidence is guessing dressed up as method. Every gap here is decided by four testable constraints — grammatical slot, collocation, polarity, and connector logic — and by nothing else.
e-cloze-mains.coreMethod:
1. READ THE WHOLE PASSAGE ONCE WITHOUT LOOKING AT ANY OPTIONS (35-40 seconds). Read gaps as silent blanks. Your only goal is the argument's SHAPE: what is the author's position, and does each paragraph support it or concede against it. Looking at options during this read is the single most expensive mistake in Mains cloze — five plausible words per gap will hijack your reading and you will finish with no sense of direction.

2. WRITE A ONE-WORD POLARITY TAG in the margin of each sentence containing a gap: '+' if the clause is favourable, '-' if unfavourable, '=' if neutral/descriptive. You will use these tags at step 6 and they cost about four seconds each.

3. IDENTIFY THE GRAMMATICAL SLOT before reading the options. Say to yourself what part of speech and what form the gap needs: singular noun / past participle / -ing form after a preposition / adverb modifying an adjective / connector joining two independent clauses. Then read the five options. In a well-set Mains item this alone kills one or two options outright — a noun offered where the slot needs a verb, or a bare infinitive where the slot follows 'by'.

4. RUN THE COLLOCATION TEST on the survivors. Take the two or three words immediately before and after the gap and ask which surviving option actually combines with them in edited English. 'Stem the FLOW', 'curb the PRACTICE', 'quell the UNREST', 'halt the PROJECT' — same meaning family, different fixed partners. The neighbouring noun or preposition is the evidence. This is the highest-yield step in Mains cloze and it is a lookup, not a judgement.

5. RUN THE PREPOSITION LOCK. If the gap is followed by a preposition already printed in the passage, that preposition alone often decides the answer: 'result IN' versus 'result FROM', 'comply WITH', 'consist OF', 'deter FROM', 'attribute TO', 'culminate IN'. Any option that does not take the printed preposition is dead regardless of meaning.

6. RUN THE POLARITY TEST using your step-2 tag. If the sentence is tagged '-' the gap word must carry negative or restrictive force; a positively-charged near-synonym is the distractor. Watch the sentence's own signposts: despite, although, yet, far from, no longer, fails to. These flip the polarity mid-sentence and the gap sits on whichever side of the flip it actually occupies.

7. FOR CONNECTOR GAPS, decide from clause structure, not from feel. Test three questions in order: are the two sides same-direction (moreover, indeed, likewise) or opposed (however, whereas, conversely, albeit)? Is the connector joining two independent clauses (however/therefore, needing a semicolon or full stop before) or subordinating one to the other (whereas/although/since, which do not)? Does it need a noun phrase after it (despite, notwithstanding) or a full clause (although, even though)? 'Despite he was late' fails on the third test alone.

8. SUBSTITUTE AND READ THE FULL SENTENCE, not the gap. Put your chosen word in and read the sentence end to end once. Mains distractors are built to look correct in a four-word window and wrong in a fifteen-word one. This read is where subject-verb agreement across a long subject, and tense consistency with a neighbouring clause, actually surface.

9. GAP-ORDER RULE: solve the easy gaps first and let them constrain the hard ones. Structural gaps (connectors, prepositions, verb forms) are usually faster than lexical ones, so sweep those first, then return to the near-synonym gaps with the argument's direction now fully visible. In a set of seven this ordering typically converts two coin-flips into decided answers.

10. STOPPING RULE per gap: 30 seconds. At 30 seconds, if you have eliminated at least two of the five options, mark the best survivor — with 0.25 negative and three options left, expected value is (1/3 x 1) + (2/3 x -0.25) = +0.17, so marking is correct. If you have eliminated fewer than two, leave it blank: a blind five-way guess has expected value exactly (1/5 x 1) + (4/5 x -0.25) = 0 and gains you nothing while it damages the accuracy you need across 40 questions.
tricks: Solve structural gaps before lexical ones. Connector, preposition and verb-form gaps are decided by syntax and typically fall in 12-18 seconds each; clearing them first hands you the paragraph's logical skeleton, which then decides the near-synonym gaps you were going to agonise over. Reordering the set this way regularly saves 30-40 seconds without changing any individual technique.

When five options are genuine near-synonyms, stop comparing their meanings and look only at the word touching the gap. 'A sharp ______ in exports' versus 'a sharp ______ of exports' will separate 'decline' from 'depletion' faster than any amount of thinking about what the sentence means.

Read the sentence AFTER the gap sentence before you commit on a connector gap. The following sentence usually continues one direction or the other, and it settles however-versus-moreover in about five seconds — far faster than re-parsing the sentence you are stuck on.

Any option that would need a different preposition from the one already printed is eliminated instantly, no meaning check required. Scan for a printed preposition immediately after the gap first — when it is there, it is the cheapest kill in the whole passage.

Mark polarity in the margin during the first read, not later. Re-deriving 'is this clause favourable or not' at the moment you are choosing between two near-synonyms costs you the reread you were trying to avoid.

If two options both survive every test, check whether one is transitive and the other intransitive against what actually follows the gap. This decides a surprising share of Mains near-synonym pairs (rise/raise, lie/lay, affect/effect used verbally) and takes three seconds.
traps: Reading the options during the first pass. Five plausible words per gap will overwrite your sense of the argument, and you finish the read knowing the vocabulary and not the direction — which is exactly backwards, since direction is what the near-synonym gaps turn on.

Choosing the most formal or most 'editorial-sounding' option. In a properly set Mains item all five come from the same register, so formality carries zero information; when it seems to work it is coincidence, and it will fail you on the items that decide your merit position.

Ignoring a mid-sentence polarity flip. 'Despite the sharp recovery, output remains ______ its pre-pandemic level' needs a word of shortfall, not of strength — candidates tag the sentence positive off the first clause and pick the positive word.

Testing the word in a four-word window. Distractors are engineered to read fine locally. Subject-verb agreement across a long subject, and tense clash with the previous clause, only appear when you read the complete sentence back.

Treating a connector gap as a vocabulary gap. 'Despite' and 'although' are not synonyms you choose between on meaning — one takes a noun phrase and one takes a clause, and the printed text after the gap already decides which.

Spending 60-70 seconds on the one gap you cannot crack. Seven gaps at 30 seconds is 210 seconds; one 70-second gap forces you to rush two others, so a single stubborn item costs you three questions rather than one.

Carrying the Prelims reflex that the odd-sounding word is the answer. Mains sets contain no obviously wrong option, so 'which one sounds most unusual' selects nothing and consumes time you needed for the collocation check.
e-cloze-mains.timeTarget: A 7-gap Mains cloze set in 210-240 seconds (3.5-4 minutes) total: 35-40 seconds for the option-free first read plus polarity tags, then an average of 25 seconds per gap, plus about 20 seconds of slack for the one gap that resists. The per-gap hard cap is 30 seconds, and 7 x 30 = 210, so the cap and the total are consistent — the slack exists because the structural gaps you clear first will come in under 20 seconds and fund the harder lexical ones. Against a 35-minute, 40-question Mains English section (2,100 seconds, about 52 seconds per question average), a 7-question set at 240 seconds is 34 seconds per question, so this set should run ahead of your section pace and buy time back for Reading Comprehension.
e-cloze-mains.masteryCheck: On a fresh 7-gap Mains-level set with a 240-second timer: you pass when you score at least 6 of 7, you never opened the options before finishing the first read, and — the part that actually tests the method — you can state for every gap which of the four constraints decided it: grammatical slot, collocation, preposition lock, or polarity. 'It sounded right' is a fail even on a correct answer, because it will not survive the next set where two options both sound right. Run this over five sets; the standard is 30 or more marks out of 35 with a named constraint behind every mark. Separately, verify you are not leaning on register: go back through your five sets and confirm you never chose an option on the grounds that it was the most formal word offered.
questionPatterns: Standard Mains gap with near-synonym options: 'The central bank moved early to ______ the build-up of speculative positions in the currency market.' (a) quell (b) curb (c) halt (d) restrain (e) stem. Answer (b) curb — the collocation is 'curb a build-up / curb speculation'; 'quell' takes unrest or rebellion, 'halt' takes a process already moving as a whole, 'restrain' takes a person or an impulse, 'stem' takes a flow or a tide.

Connector gap decided by clause structure: 'Rural credit off-take rose by nine per cent, ______ urban credit growth slipped to its lowest level in three years.' (a) despite (b) whereas (c) therefore (d) notwithstanding (e) in spite of. Answer (b) whereas — the gap joins two full clauses in opposition; despite, notwithstanding and in spite of all require a noun phrase, not a clause, and therefore is same-direction.

Preposition-locked gap: 'The shortfall in collections has been ______ to weaker festive demand and an unusually long monsoon.' (a) blamed (b) attributed (c) accounted (d) credited (e) assigned. Answer (b) attributed — 'attributed TO' is the fixed pairing; 'blamed ON', 'accounted FOR', and 'credited' carries positive polarity that clashes with a shortfall.

Polarity-flip gap: 'Despite three consecutive quarters of recovery, factory output remains ______ its pre-pandemic level.' (a) beyond (b) above (c) below (d) around (e) exceeding. Answer (c) below — 'Despite' flips the direction, so the main clause must state a shortfall.

Verb-form / transitivity gap: 'The scheme is expected to ______ employment across the textile clusters of Tiruppur and Surat.' (a) rise (b) arise (c) raise (d) rouse (e) arouse. Answer (c) raise — the gap takes a direct object ('employment'), which rules out the intransitive rise and arise; rouse and arouse do not combine with employment.

e-cloze-mains.aiPrompt: Create 3 IBPS Clerk Mains level cloze test sets. Each set: one 170-200 word argumentative passage on Indian monetary policy, fiscal consolidation, climate finance, MSME credit or labour formalisation, containing exactly SEVEN numbered gaps. Every gap must have exactly FIVE options labelled (a) to (e). Design the seven gaps to this mix: two gaps where all five options are near-synonyms separated ONLY by collocation with the adjacent noun or preposition; two gaps decided by a preposition already printed after the blank; one connector gap where the wrong options fail because they need a noun phrase while the text supplies a full clause (or vice versa); one polarity gap where the sentence contains despite / although / far from so the correct word runs against the surface reading; one gap decided by transitivity or verb form. Constraint: all five options in every item must sit in the SAME register — do not make the correct answer identifiable by being the most formal or most editorial word, and do not include any obviously wrong or comic option. Then give an answer key in which each explanation names exactly which constraint decides the item — grammatical slot, collocation, preposition lock, polarity, or connector structure — and states why each of the four wrong options dies. Verify every item has exactly one defensible answer before you output it.
e-cloze-mains.blockPlan: This topic belongs to your Mains phase, but the collocation reflex it builds is slow to grow, so start it lightly early. From now to Prelims (Oct 2026), 15 minutes twice a week inside your English hour: one 7-gap set untimed, then a full review where you write the deciding constraint next to every gap. Also keep a running collocation sheet — one line per near-synonym cluster you meet (curb/stem/quell/halt/restrain, decline/depletion/erosion/slump/dip) with the noun each one actually takes. Twenty minutes of building that sheet is worth more than two extra practice sets. Post-Prelims (mid-Oct to 27 Dec), raise to 30 minutes four days a week: two timed 240-second sets plus 10 minutes revising the collocation sheet. In the final three weeks, drop new sets and revise only the sheet plus your logged errors — at that stage the marginal mark comes from recall speed, not from new exposure.

e-phrase.whatItIs:
A sentence is printed with one phrase in bold or underlined. Five options follow: four alternative phrasings plus, in almost every Clerk-level item, a version of 'No correction required' or 'No replacement required'. You decide whether the bold phrase is correct as it stands, and if not, which alternative fixes it.

Banks also print this as 'Sentence Improvement' and, in a closely related shape, as 'Correct/Incorrect Sentences'. The skill is identical.

The crucial difference from a general grammar question is that the whole sentence is not up for debate — only the bold phrase is. Everything outside the bold is stipulated correct and functions as your evidence. If the bold phrase contains a verb, the subject sitting outside the bold tells you what number and person it must take. If it contains a preposition, the noun outside tells you which preposition is required. Candidates who try to fix the whole sentence lose time and sometimes reject a correct bold phrase because something outside it looked odd.

The planted errors come from a short, closed list, which is why this topic converts to reliable marks faster than most: subject-verb agreement (usually with a distractor between subject and verb, or a neither/nor or either/or construction); tense sequence across two clauses; parallelism in a list or in a not-only/but-also pair; wrong preposition in a fixed phrase; misplaced or dangling modifier; article errors; comparative and superlative form; and redundancy ('return back', 'repeat again', 'more better', 'cope up with').
e-phrase.coreMethod:
1. READ THE ENTIRE SENTENCE, INCLUDING WHAT IS OUTSIDE THE BOLD, ONCE (6-8 seconds). The evidence for judging the bold phrase is almost always outside it. Reading only the bold is the fastest way to get this topic wrong.

2. LOCATE THE TRUE SUBJECT OF THE BOLD VERB, if the bold contains a verb. Cross out any intervening prepositional phrase — 'the list of approved vendors', 'a bundle of documents', 'one of the branches' — because the subject is the head noun before 'of', not the noun after it. Then apply the specific rules: with 'neither A nor B' and 'either A or B', the verb agrees with the nearer subject (the proximity rule); 'one of the X who' takes a plural verb in the relative clause; collective nouns in Indian banking usage normally take a singular verb.

3. RUN THE SIX-CHECK SWEEP ON THE BOLD PHRASE, in this order, stopping at the first failure. (i) AGREEMENT: does the verb match the true subject in number and person? (ii) TENSE: is the bold's tense consistent with the tense outside it, and with any time marker printed in the sentence? (iii) PREPOSITION: is every preposition inside the bold the one its partner word takes? (iv) PARALLELISM: if the bold sits in a list, or after not only / either / both, does its form match the other elements? (v) MODIFIER: if the bold is a participial phrase, does the noun immediately following it actually perform that action? (vi) REDUNDANCY: does the bold repeat meaning already present (return back, revert back, repeat again, more easier, cope up with, discuss about)?

4. FORM YOUR VERDICT BEFORE READING THE OPTIONS. Write 'OK' or the name of the failed check in the margin. Reading five rewrites first will make a correct bold phrase look doubtful and costs you 10-15 seconds of relitigation per item.

5. IF YOUR VERDICT IS 'OK', mark 'No correction required' and move on. Do not overrule your own sweep because the alternatives look elegant. Alternatives are written to be attractive and to introduce a second, subtler error.

6. IF YOUR VERDICT IS A FAILED CHECK, use that check as the filter rather than comparing all four rewrites. Failed on agreement: keep only options with the right verb number. Failed on preposition: keep only options with the right preposition. This is where the speed in this topic comes from — one filter instead of four comparisons.

7. CHECK EACH SURVIVOR FOR A SECOND PLANTED ERROR. The standard construction offers one option that fixes the stated error and simultaneously breaks the preposition, the number, or the tense. In the worked pattern below, the option that corrects 'was' to 'were' but also changes 'aware of' to 'aware about' is exactly this trap.

8. SUBSTITUTE AND READ THE WHOLE SENTENCE BACK once. The rewrite must fit the words on both sides of the bold, not just read well by itself.

9. STOPPING RULE: 25 seconds. At the cap, mark only if two or more options are eliminated — three survivors against 0.25 negative gives expected value (1/3 x 1) + (2/3 x -0.25) = +0.17. Fewer than two eliminated means leave it blank, since a blind five-way guess is worth exactly (1/5 x 1) + (4/5 x -0.25) = 0 and buys nothing.
tricks: Cross out every prepositional phrase between the subject and the bold verb before you judge agreement. 'The list of approved vendors', 'a set of guidelines', 'one of the officers' — the singular head noun is the subject, and physically striking the intervening words removes the illusion in about three seconds.

Decide on the bold phrase before you read the five options, every time. This is the same discipline the replacement-type cloze needs, and it is worth 10-15 seconds per item here because it turns four comparisons into one filtered lookup.

When the bold contains a preposition, check it against its partner word first — it is the cheapest kill available and often reduces five options to two before you consider anything else. Keep a running list: aware of, comply with, deter from, averse to, comprise (no 'of'), discuss (no 'about'), superior to, prefer to, consist of.

For neither/nor and either/or constructions, apply the proximity rule mechanically: the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it, so 'Neither the manager nor the clerks were…' and 'Neither the clerks nor the manager was…' are both correct. Setters use this pair constantly and it resolves in two seconds once it is automatic.

Scan for redundancy words as a fixed short list rather than judging by ear: return back, revert back, repeat again, more better, most easiest, cope up with, discuss about, enter into (a room), reason because. Any of these inside the bold is an instant fail, no analysis needed.

If the bold starts with an -ing or -ed participle, look immediately at the noun right after the comma. If that noun cannot perform the participle's action, the modifier is dangling and the bold fails — this single look decides the whole item.
traps: Judging the bold phrase in isolation. The controlling subject, the governing preposition and the comparison partner all typically sit outside the bold, so a candidate who reads only the underlined words is choosing without the evidence.

Selecting an option that fixes the obvious error and introduces a quiet one. This is the topic's signature construction: the rewrite corrects the verb number but swaps 'aware of' for 'aware about', or corrects the tense but pluralises a noun that must stay singular. Skipping the substitute-and-read-back step is what lets it through.

Rejecting 'No correction required' because five options are offered and one of them must surely be better. Treating that option as a decoy is a policy, not a check, and with 0.25 negative it costs marks on every correctly-printed item.
Being pulled by the noun nearest the verb in an of-phrase. 'A bundle of documents were dispatched' reads naturally and is wrong; the subject is 'bundle'.
Applying the proximity rule to and-joined subjects. 'The manager and the clerk was informed' is wrong — proximity governs neither/nor and either/or only, and 'and' always makes a plural subject.

Reading the rewrites as free-standing sentences. An option can be flawless in itself and still clash with the fixed words on either side of the bold, so the read-back must include the surrounding text.
Trying to fix the whole sentence. Everything outside the bold is stipulated correct; arguing with it wastes 15-20 seconds and occasionally causes candidates to replace a bold phrase that was fine.

Breakdown per item: 6-8 seconds reading the full sentence, 6-8 seconds running the sweep and writing your verdict, 5-8 seconds filtering the options and reading back. Hard cap 25 seconds. Against the 40-second-per-question average in a 20-minute, 30-question Prelims section, this topic should run comfortably ahead of pace and contribute time to your Reading Comprehension budget. In Mains, phrase replacement and its Correct/Incorrect-sentence cousin sit at the same 20-25 seconds; the sentences are longer but the error list is the same, so the sweep does not lengthen — only the initial read does, by about 3 seconds.
e-phrase.masteryCheck: On a fresh 10-question mixed set with a 4-minute timer: pass at 9 of 10, subject to three process conditions. First, you wrote 'OK' or a named failed check in the margin BEFORE uncovering the options on every item — verify by physically covering the option list with your hand until your verdict is written. Second, your accuracy on items whose answer is 'No correction required' is within one mark of your accuracy on items needing a rewrite; a persistent gap means you are running a policy about that option rather than a sweep, and the paper is built to punish exactly that. Third, on every item you got wrong you can name which of the six checks you skipped. Run this weekly. A useful additional drill: take ten items you answered correctly and, for each, state what second error the most attractive wrong option contained — if you cannot, you are picking the right answer without seeing the trap, and that will not hold on harder sentences.
questionPatterns: Proximity rule with a second planted error in the alternatives: 'Neither the manager nor the clerks WAS AWARE OF THE REVISED GUIDELINE.' Options: (a) were aware of the revised guideline (b) was aware about the revised guideline (c) were aware for the revised guidelines (d) No correction required (e) has been aware of the revised guideline. Answer (a) — proximity makes the verb agree with 'clerks', so it must be 'were'; (b) fixes nothing and breaks the preposition, (c) breaks the preposition and changes the number of the noun, (e) is singular.

Intervening of-phrase: 'The list of approved vendors HAVE BEEN CIRCULATED to all branches.' Options: (a) has been circulated (b) have circulated (c) are being circulated (d) No correction required (e) had circulated. Answer (a) — the subject is 'list', not 'vendors', so the verb is singular; (b) and (e) also switch to the active voice, which the sentence does not support.

Bold phrase correct as printed: 'The committee comprises five members drawn from three departments.' with COMPRISES FIVE MEMBERS in bold. Options: (a) comprises of five members (b) is comprised five members (c) No correction required (d) comprise of five members (e) are comprising five members. Answer (c) — 'comprise' does not take 'of', so every rewrite introduces an error.

Dangling modifier: 'HAVING SUBMITTED THE APPLICATION LATE, the branch rejected his claim.' Options: (a) Having submitted the application late, his claim was rejected by the branch (b) Since he had submitted the application late, the branch rejected his claim (c) No correction required (d) Submitting the application late, the branch rejected his claim (e) Being submitted late, the branch rejected his claim. Answer (b) — the participle must attach to the person who submitted, and only (b) restructures so the subject of the action is 'he'; (a) and (d) and (e) leave the modifier dangling on the wrong noun.

Parallelism: 'The new scheme aims at reducing paperwork, to speed up disbursement AND SIMPLIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY NORMS.' Options: (a) and simplifying eligibility norms (b) and to simplify eligibility norms (c) No correction required (d) and simplified eligibility norms (e) and simplify of eligibility norms. Answer (a) — the list is governed by 'aims at', which takes -ing forms, so all three items must be gerunds; note this also means the printed 'to speed up' is non-parallel, but it lies outside the bold and is therefore stipulated as given.

e-phrase-swap.whatItIs: A sentence containing three or four bold PHRASES that have been shuffled out of position. You choose which two phrases must be interchanged to make the sentence coherent. It is a grammatical slot-matching puzzle, not a comprehension task.
e-phrase-swap.coreMethod:
1. Read the sentence once at normal pace. Do not try to repair it yet — only register WHERE the sentence stops making sense. That location is your entry point.
2. Extract the skeleton: subject + main verb + object. If a bold phrase is occupying the subject slot but is obviously object-type material (or vice versa), you have one end of the swap.
3. MATCH BY GRAMMATICAL SLOT, which is the core of the method. A prepositional phrase can only swap with another prepositional phrase. A noun phrase with a noun phrase. A verb phrase with a verb phrase. Any option pairing two phrases of different grammatical type is almost certainly wrong, and this single rule kills most of the option list before you think about meaning.
4. Then match by SEMANTIC FIT. Read the sentence with just that one pair interchanged. If it reads clean from start to finish, mark it. You should need at most two trial substitutions.
5. When testing a pair, read ONLY the two affected clauses, not the whole sentence. Re-reading a 30-word sentence four times is where the time goes.
6. If two pairs both appear to work, choose the one that fixes the EARLIEST point of incoherence. IBPS builds these so that exactly one interchange repairs the entire sentence.
tricks: Work backwards from the OPTION LIST, not from the sentence. There are only four or five candidate pairs on offer; testing pairs is far faster than diagnosing the sentence unaided. Test first the pair whose two phrases are most similar in grammatical shape.

The two phrases that must move are almost always WRONG for where they sit but IDENTICAL in grammatical role to each other. If two bold phrases both open with the same preposition ('in the...', 'in the...'), or both are '-ing' phrases, they are prime candidates — spot them by shape before reading a word of meaning.

Look for the phrase producing obvious nonsense — an abstract noun performing a physical action, a time expression in a place slot. That phrase is one half of the pair; find its partner purely by slot type.

You do not need to know what the sentence is about. Slot-matching is topic-blind, which means an unfamiliar subject (macroeconomics, marine biology) costs you nothing. Do not let unfamiliar vocabulary make you skip this question.

Check the words immediately BORDERING each bold phrase. Those border words determine what grammatical type belongs there, and reading four pairs of border words is faster than reading the sentence twice.
traps: Trying to repair the sentence in your head before looking at the options. The options constrain you to four specific pairs — use that constraint, it is a gift.
Choosing a swap that fixes the first half and quietly breaks the second. Always read PAST the swap point to the end of the sentence.
Assuming three phrases are out of place. In this format exactly TWO move, unless an option explicitly states otherwise.
Being scared off by unknown vocabulary. The method never requires you to know a single word's meaning.
Ignoring a 'no interchange required' option where one is offered — occasionally the sentence is already correct and the reflex to swap something costs a quarter mark.
Confusing this with word swap and looking at single words. Here the unit is a multi-word phrase, and single-word comparisons will produce nonsense.
e-phrase-swap.timeTarget: 25-35 seconds per question. Slower than single-word swap because each phrase is longer to re-read — budget honestly rather than assuming word-swap pace.
e-phrase-swap.masteryCheck: You can solve a four-phrase swap question by testing at most TWO option pairs, in under 30 seconds, on 8 of 10 questions — and you can state the grammatical type (prepositional / noun / verb phrase) of all four bold phrases.

e-fillers.whatItIs:
A standalone sentence with one blank (single filler) or two blanks (double filler), followed by five options. In the double-filler format each option is a PAIR of words and both halves must fit — a pair whose first word is perfect and whose second word fails is wrong, which is what makes double fillers a different exercise from doing two single fillers.

Unlike cloze, there is no shared passage and no accumulated context. Everything you need is inside one sentence, which cuts both ways: the item is self-contained and fast, but there is no surrounding text to rescue you if the vocabulary is unfamiliar.

The blanks are decided by a small set of forces and almost never by pure dictionary meaning. In practice: a connector or contrast word in the sentence fixing the direction (although, despite, while, yet, since, because); a fixed collocation with the word touching the blank; a preposition already printed that only some options take; grammatical form — tense, number, participle, transitivity; and, in double fillers, agreement between the two blanks, since the pair usually has to run in one consistent direction.

At Clerk level this is one of the cheapest topics per mark on the paper: no reading cost, no chain to build, and each item resolves in well under half a minute once the checks are automatic. It is a good topic to place early in your section run because it banks marks and steadies the clock before you commit to Reading Comprehension.
e-fillers.coreMethod:
1. READ THE SENTENCE ONCE, ALL THE WAY THROUGH, BEFORE LOOKING AT THE OPTIONS (5-7 seconds). The temptation to read blank-then-options is strong because the sentence is short; resist it, because the deciding evidence is usually in the clause AFTER the blank.

2. FIND THE DIRECTION WORD AND CIRCLE IT. Scan for although, though, even though, despite, in spite of, while, whereas, yet, but, however, on the contrary (all contrast) and because, since, as, therefore, thus, hence, so, moreover (all same-direction). One of these is present in a large share of filler items, and when it is present it fixes the relationship between the two halves of the sentence before you have considered a single option.

3. NAME WHAT THE BLANK NEEDS. Part of speech first, then form: singular or plural noun; past tense or past participle; -ing form because a preposition precedes; adverb because it modifies an adjective; comparative because 'than' follows. Do this out of your own head, not by inspecting the options.

4. NOW READ THE OPTIONS AND KILL ON FORM. Any option in the wrong word class, wrong tense against a time marker in the sentence ('last quarter' forces past), wrong number against a following noun, or a bare verb where a participle is needed, dies immediately without any meaning check. At Clerk level this typically removes two of the five.

5. KILL ON DIRECTION using your circled word. If the sentence says 'Although profits fell sharply, the share price ______', the second half must NOT continue the fall. Options that agree with the first clause when the sentence demands contrast are out.

6. KILL ON PREPOSITION. If a preposition is printed next to the blank, keep only options that take it: 'refrain FROM', 'comply WITH', 'result IN', 'deter FROM', 'immune TO', 'consist OF', 'averse TO', 'conducive TO'. This is a lookup, not a judgement, and it is often the fastest single elimination available.

7. DECIDE THE LAST TWO ON COLLOCATION. Read the three words either side of the blank and ask which survivor genuinely partners with them: 'certify the accounts', 'address a shortfall', 'bridge a gap', 'stem a flow', 'levy a fine', 'incur a loss'. The adjacent noun is the evidence.

8. DOUBLE-FILLER RULE — TEST THE SECOND BLANK FIRST. Option-setters make the first word of several pairs look plausible and put the discriminating evidence in the second blank. Working right-to-left kills three or four pairs in one sweep, whereas working left-to-right leaves you comparing three surviving pairs on the first word alone. Then confirm the surviving pair's first word.

9. DOUBLE-FILLER CONSISTENCY CHECK. Once a pair survives, read the complete sentence with both words in and check that the two halves relate the way the direction word demands. A pair can pass both blanks individually and still make the sentence contradict its own 'although'.

10. STOPPING RULE: 20 seconds on a single filler, 30 on a double. At the cap, mark only if you have eliminated at least two options — three survivors against 0.25 negative gives expected value (1/3 x 1) + (2/3 x -0.25) = +0.17. With fewer than two eliminated, leave it blank; a blind five-way guess is worth exactly (1/5 x 1) + (4/5 x -0.25) = 0, so it cannot raise your score and it will lower your accuracy.
tricks: On double fillers, always attack the SECOND blank first. The setter loads plausibility into the first word of several pairs and puts the real discriminator in the second, so right-to-left commonly reduces five pairs to one in a single sweep — this is worth 8-10 seconds per item and is the single biggest speed gain in the topic.

Circle the direction word before you read any option. 'Although', 'despite', 'while' and 'yet' each decide the relationship between the halves of the sentence on their own, and knowing the required direction before you see the options stops the options from talking you out of it.
If a preposition is printed beside the blank, use it first. It is a pure lookup with no thinking attached and it frequently cuts five options to two before meaning enters the picture at all.

Check the time marker against the verb form. 'last quarter', 'in 2024', 'since March', 'by next year' each lock a tense, and an option in the wrong tense is dead regardless of how well it fits the meaning — this resolves many items in under five seconds.

Keep a two-column collocation sheet — verb on the left, the nouns it takes on the right (levy: fine, tax, duty / incur: loss, cost, penalty / certify: accounts, results, documents / stem: flow, tide, outflow). Fillers recycle these pairings across shifts far more than they recycle rare vocabulary.

Do fillers early in your Prelims English run. They are the lowest-variance marks in the section, so banking them first steadies your clock before Reading Comprehension, which is the section's only genuinely open-ended time risk.
traps: On a double filler, selecting a pair because the first word is clearly right. Both halves must fit; the setter's standard construction is two or three pairs sharing an excellent first word and differing only in the second. Left-to-right reading walks straight into this.

Missing the contrast word. 'Although the bank's profits fell sharply, its share price fell too' is a sentence candidates mark as correct because each half sounds fine — the 'although' makes it self-contradictory, and it is missed because it sits at the very start of the sentence where the eye is already moving.

Reading only up to the blank. In many filler items the deciding evidence — the preposition, the following noun, the 'than', the second clause — sits after the blank, so a candidate who stops reading at the gap is choosing on incomplete information.

Ignoring transitivity. 'The policy is expected to ______ employment' takes an object, which rules out rise and arise no matter how well they fit the sense; candidates decide on meaning and never test whether the verb can take what follows.

Confusing tense-plausible with tense-correct. 'Profits have fallen last quarter' feels acceptable when read quickly; the definite past marker forbids the present perfect, and this construction appears often enough to be worth a dedicated check.

Treating fillers as a vocabulary test and skipping them when the words look unfamiliar. Most Clerk-level filler items are decided by direction, form, preposition or collocation — you can eliminate three options without knowing what one of them means.

Over-investing because the item is short. A sentence that takes ten seconds to read invites you to keep re-reading it; at 45 seconds a single filler has cost you the same as two, with no more information than you had at fifteen.

questionPatterns: Double filler, contrast-driven: 'Although the bank's profits ______ sharply last quarter, its share price ______ almost unchanged.' Options: (a) fell / remained (b) rose / rose (c) dropped / dropping (d) fall / remains (e) fallen / remained. Answer (a) — 'Although' demands contrast, which kills (b); (c) needs a finite verb after 'share price'; (d) clashes with the past marker 'last quarter'; (e) has a bare participle with no auxiliary.

Single filler, collocation-driven: 'The auditor refused to ______ the accounts until the discrepancies were explained.' Options: (a) certify (b) clarify (c) classify (d) codify (e) crucify. Answer (a) certify — 'certify the accounts' is the fixed pairing; the other four do not take 'accounts' in this sense.

Single filler, preposition-locked: 'New recruits are expected to refrain ______ discussing internal matters on social media.' Options: (a) of (b) from (c) with (d) against (e) for. Answer (b) from — 'refrain from' is fixed, and no meaning judgement is required.

Single filler, transitivity: 'The revised policy is expected to ______ rural employment by nearly twelve per cent.' Options: (a) rise (b) arise (c) raise (d) arouse (e) rouse. Answer (c) raise — the blank takes a direct object, ruling out the intransitive rise and arise; arouse and rouse do not combine with employment.

Double filler, same-direction: 'Because the monsoon arrived ______ this year, reservoir levels across the state were ______ than the ten-year average.' Options: (a) early / higher (b) late / higher (c) early / lower (d) heavily / high (e) early / highest. Answer (a) — 'Because' demands the halves agree; (b) and (c) invert the causal link, (d) fails on 'than' which requires a comparative, and (e) uses a superlative where 'than' requires a comparative.

e-parajumble.whatItIs:
A short paragraph is split into five sentences labelled (A) to (E) and printed in scrambled order. What matters for method is the ANSWER FORMAT, and it is not the format most practice books teach. IBPS Clerk does not ask you to pick a correct sequence string. It asks FIVE separate questions off the same paragraph, each of the form 'Which of the following is the THIRD sentence after rearrangement?', and the five options for every one of those questions are just the sentence labels: (a) A (b) B (c) C (d) D (e) E. There is no 'BCADE / BACDE / CBADE' option list anywhere on the screen.

The consequence is the whole reason this topic needs its own method. Because the options are single labels, there is nothing to eliminate against and no candidate ordering to test. Back-solving is structurally unavailable. You must construct the one correct chain yourself, from scratch, and only then can you answer anything. In exchange, once the chain is built, all five questions are free — they are five readings of one line you have already written.

So the set behaves as a block, not as five independent questions. A correct chain earns 5 marks in roughly two minutes, which is the best marks-per-minute rate available in the English section. A chain that is right at the ends but scrambled in the middle typically gets positions 1 and 5 right and loses three questions at 0.25 each. Your training target is therefore chain accuracy, not question accuracy.

Variants you will meet: the six-sentence version (A) to (F); the fixed-opener version, where the paper states 'Sentence (A) is fixed as the first sentence' and you order only the remaining four or five; and, in Mains, sentence-rearrangement sets that sit alongside connector and column-matching items.
e-parajumble.coreMethod:
1. FIRST PASS (about 25 seconds). Read all five sentences once. You are not reading for topic — you never need to know what the paragraph is about. Mark three things on the paper: the first word of each sentence, every pronoun and demonstrative (it, its, they, their, this, these, such, he, she), and the article sitting in front of each key noun (a/an versus the).

2. FIND THE OPENER BY EXCLUSION, not by feel. Strike out any sentence that cannot be first because it contains: (i) a pronoun or demonstrative whose antecedent is not inside that same sentence; (ii) a fronted connector of contrast, addition or result — However, But, Yet, Instead, Also, Moreover, Besides, Therefore, Thus, So, Hence, Meanwhile, On the contrary; (iii) 'the' on a noun that is being introduced for the first time in the paragraph; (iv) a comparative (better, larger, more so) with nothing to compare to. Usually one sentence survives. If two survive, the opener is the one that names the subject in FULL (complete proper noun or full noun phrase) while the other names it in short form.

3. BUILD THE ARTICLE CHAIN — your strongest link. If one sentence contains 'a three-district pilot' and another contains 'The pilot', edited English forces indefinite BEFORE definite. This is a grammatical constraint, not a preference. Do the same for 'a scheme … the scheme', 'an audit … the audit'. Write each finding in the margin as an arrow: A→E.

4. BUILD THE PRONOUN CHAIN. Every It / They / This / Its / He must come after a full noun of matching number and gender. 'They' cannot point back to 'the scheme'; 'it' cannot point back to 'the farmers'. Each match gives you one more arrow. Note this gives ORDER (X before Y), never a fixed position.

5. BUILD THE CONNECTOR AND TIME CHAIN. However / But / Instead / On the contrary must sit immediately after the exact claim they reverse — find that claim, not just any earlier sentence. Also / Moreover / In addition sit after a same-direction claim. Therefore / Thus / As a result sit after the cause. Then sort any time markers you find: initially, first, at first, later, subsequently, since then, now, finally. A timeline is a total ordering and often finishes the chain by itself.

6. ASSEMBLE. You now have arrows like B→C, C→A, A→E. Merge them into one sequence and see which label is left over — that is your closer. If two fragments will not join, the missing link is almost always an article or a time word you have not used yet; re-scan only for those two things, not for meaning.

7. ONE VERIFY READ (about 15 seconds). Read the assembled paragraph in order. It must run as continuous prose with no dangling reference and no repeated introduction. If exactly one sentence feels inserted, swap it with a neighbour and re-read. Do this once. A second swap-and-reread almost always costs more time than the marks at stake.

8. WRITE THE ORDER DOWN, then answer. In the margin write '1B 2C 3A 4E 5D'. Read each question's ordinal, read the answer straight off that line, mark it. Do not re-derive anything per question and do not re-open the sentences.

9. CUT-OFF RULE at 2 minutes 15 seconds. If the middle is still unresolved, mark only the positions you have actually established (the opener and closer are derived independently of the middle by steps 2 and 5, so you usually still own those two) and leave the rest blank. With five options and 0.25 negative marking, a blind guess has expected value (1/5 x 1) + (4/5 x -0.25) = exactly 0 — it buys you nothing. Only mark an unresolved position if you have genuinely eliminated at least two labels, at which point the expected value turns positive.
tricks: The indefinite-to-definite article chain is the most mechanical link in the whole topic: 'a QR code' in one sentence and 'the code' in another fixes their order with no judgement required. Hunt for it before you read for sense — it typically resolves one link in under five seconds.

Write '1_ 2_ 3_ 4_ 5_' in the margin BEFORE you start solving and fill slots out of order as certainty arrives. The opener (step 2, exclusion) and the closer (forward-looking language: 'now expect', 'is likely to', 'by next March') are each derivable without knowing the middle, so you can bank two slots while still working on positions 2-4.

When the paper says a sentence is fixed as the first, question one is already answered — skip straight to chaining the remainder and you have effectively bought yourself 20 seconds for the harder middle.

Never summarise the paragraph. Ordering is a reference-and-grammar task. Candidates who try to reconstruct the author's argument spend 40 extra seconds and land on the same chain the article rule gave for free.

On the six-sentence variant the pairwise work roughly doubles, so lock positions 1 and 6 first and treat the middle four as a smaller sub-problem — this keeps you inside the same time budget instead of blowing it by a minute.

Read the five question ordinals BEFORE you start solving. They arrive shuffled, and knowing that today's set asks FOURTH, SECOND, FIFTH, FIRST, THIRD stops you from marking answers positionally down the screen out of habit.
traps: Arriving with the wrong format in your head. Aspirants trained on 'choose the correct sequence: (a) BCADE (b) BACDE …' spend 15-20 seconds scanning for sequence options that do not exist, then panic-mark. In IBPS Clerk every option is one letter, and no elimination-against-options technique applies.

Mis-matching the ordinal. The five stems are printed in shuffled ordinal order. Reading your chain's SECOND sentence against the stem that actually asks for the FOURTH costs two questions instantly and often cascades through the rest of the set.

Linking on repeated topic words instead of on reference. Two sentences that both contain 'bank' tell you nothing about order. 'a bank' followed by 'the bank' tells you everything. Candidates chain on the noun and get the direction backwards.

Assuming 'However' opens the second half of the paragraph. However only guarantees that it follows the specific claim it reverses — that claim may be sentence one, three or four. Placing it at a fixed slot by habit is the most common single-link error in this topic.

Ignoring pronoun number or gender because the sentence 'sounds fine'. If your chain makes 'they' refer to a singular noun, the chain is wrong somewhere earlier — fix it rather than accepting the position.

Solving the five questions one at a time, re-reading the sentences for each. This roughly triples the time for the same five marks and is the main reason candidates report para jumbles as 'slow' when the chain itself took 60 seconds.

Treating a wrong middle as a partial success. Because the marks arrive in blocks, a chain with two sentences transposed costs three questions (0.75 negative plus three unearned marks). Chain accuracy, not per-question feel, is the metric.
e-parajumble.timeTarget: A five-sentence set (all five questions) in 110-130 seconds total: about 25 seconds first pass, 45-55 seconds building and merging the arrows, 15 seconds verify read, 20-25 seconds marking all five answers off the written order. That is roughly 25 seconds per question against a 40-second average for the 20-minute, 30-question Prelims section — para jumbles should be a net time-maker for you, not a time sink. Six-sentence variant: 150-170 seconds. Fixed-opener variant: 95-110 seconds. Hard stop for the chain is 2 minutes 15 seconds, after which you mark only what you have established.
e-parajumble.masteryCheck: Take a fresh five-sentence set with a 130-second timer running. You have mastered it when all three hold: (1) the complete order is written in your margin within 75 seconds; (2) you answer all five position questions from that written line without re-opening a single sentence; (3) across ten consecutive sets your ALL-FIVE-CORRECT rate is at least 7 out of 10. Point (3) is the real test — because the marks come in blocks of five, a run where you 'usually get 3 or 4 right' is a failing score even though it feels acceptable. Additionally, on any set you get wrong, you must be able to name the specific link you broke — article, pronoun, connector or timeline — in one sentence. If you cannot name it, you guessed the chain rather than derived it.
questionPatterns: Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) in the proper sequence to form a meaningful paragraph, then answer the question. 'Which of the following is the SECOND sentence after rearrangement?' Options: (a) A (b) B (c) C (d) D (e) E.

Same paragraph, next question in the set: 'Which of the following is the FIFTH (LAST) sentence after rearrangement?' Options: (a) A (b) B (c) C (d) D (e) E. Note the ordinals across the five questions arrive shuffled, not in order 1-2-3-4-5.

Fixed-opener variant: 'Sentence (A) is fixed as the FIRST sentence of the paragraph. Rearrange sentences (B), (C), (D), (E) and (F) to form a meaningful paragraph. Which of the following is the FOURTH sentence after rearrangement?' Options: (a) B (b) C (c) D (d) E (e) F.
Six-sentence variant: 'Rearrange (A) to (F) into a coherent paragraph. Which of the following is the THIRD sentence after rearrangement?' Options: (a) A (b) B (c) C (d) D (e) F.

Worked set to check your own method (this one resolves): (A) However, the scheme was extended to rural branches after a three-district pilot. (B) The Reserve Bank of India announced a new doorstep banking scheme in March. (C) It was initially available only at urban branches of public sector banks. (D) Officials now expect the model to cover every district by next March. (E) The pilot showed that demand was highest among pensioners and senior citizens. Correct order: B, C, A, E, D. Derivation — B is the only sentence with no outward reference and the full name 'The Reserve Bank of India'; C's 'It' points to the scheme and 'initially' promises a change; A's 'However' reverses 'only at urban branches' and introduces 'a three-district pilot'; E's definite 'The pilot' must follow that indefinite mention; D closes with forward-looking 'now expect … by next March'. So THIRD = (a) A, FIRST = (b) B, FIFTH = (d) D.

e-sent-rearr.whatItIs: Fragments of a SINGLE sentence, labelled A/B/C/D or P/Q/R/S, that must be assembled into one grammatical sentence. Distinct from para jumbles: here grammar decides the order, not logic, which makes it faster once you recognise the difference.
e-sent-rearr.coreMethod:
1. Identify the unit first. If the pieces are complete sentences, it is a para jumble and logic rules. If the pieces are fragments that cannot stand alone, it is sentence rearrangement and GRAMMAR rules. Making this call in the first three seconds changes your whole approach.
2. Locate the fragment holding the MAIN VERB together with its subject. That is the spine of the sentence.
3. Find the fragment that can legally START. It cannot begin with a relative pronoun (which / who / that / whose), cannot begin with a coordinating conjunction that requires a preceding clause (and / but / so / or), cannot begin with a preposition-dependent phrase needing a prior noun, and if capitalisation is printed, must carry the capital.
4. CHAIN BY GRAMMATICAL HOOKS — this is the actual technique and it is a jigsaw with visible tabs:
   - a fragment ENDING in a preposition (in, of, with, to, for) must be followed by a noun phrase
   - a fragment ENDING in an article (a, an, the) must be followed by a noun or adjective
   - a fragment ENDING in 'that / which / who' must be followed by a verb phrase
   - a fragment STARTING with an '-ing' form attaches to the clause containing its subject
   - a fragment ENDING in a comma attaches to a clause, not a fragment
   - a fragment containing the sentence's only full stop is last
5. Assemble by hooks, then verify subject-verb agreement at every join.
6. Cross-check against the options and eliminate. If three of five options share the same opening fragment, start from that fragment and only decide the tail.
tricks: Read the FIRST and LAST word of every fragment before you read anything else. Write them down if the paper allows. Dangling prepositions, articles and relative pronouns at fragment edges lock the order without any comprehension — this converts the question from reading to matching and typically halves the time.
Punctuation is a free hook. A fragment ending in a comma is subordinate; a fragment carrying the full stop is terminal; a fragment with a semicolon splits two independent clauses.
The longest fragment containing subject + verb + object is usually the main clause and sits either first or immediately after an introductory phrase. Anchor there.
Read only the JOINS, never the whole assembled sentence during solving. You need each junction to be grammatical; the global meaning takes care of itself. Save one full read for final confirmation.
If two options survive, compare only the single position where they differ rather than re-reading both complete orders.
traps: Treating it as a para jumble and hunting for logical flow. Grammar decides it, and logic-hunting doubles the time.
Choosing an order that joins smoothly but produces two main verbs with no conjunction between them — the result is grammatical-sounding rubble, not a sentence.
Ignoring printed capitalisation when it is shown; it hands you the opener free.
Not verifying that the finished sentence has one complete subject and one main verb. A common wrong answer is a well-glued fragment pile that is not a sentence at all.
Reading fragments for vocabulary. The answer lives at the fragment edges, not in the content words.
Confusing the labelling conventions — some papers fix the first and last portions and ask you to order only the middle. Read the instruction line before solving.
e-sent-rearr.timeTarget: 30-40 seconds per question in Prelims; 35-45 seconds in Mains where fragments run longer. A 4-question block should close in 2 to 2.5 minutes.

e-wordswap.whatItIs: A sentence with four bold words labelled A-D, two of which have been interchanged. You pick the pair to swap back. It is a pure collocation test disguised as comprehension, and it is topic-blind — you never need to know what the sentence is about.
e-wordswap.coreMethod:
1. Read the sentence once. Identify the bold word that produces the loudest nonsense — you almost always notice one immediately ('he viewed the guitar' when 'played' belongs there). That word is your ANCHOR.
2. Find the anchor's correct home. Scan the other three bold positions and ask 'which slot actually needs this word?' That question gives you the pair directly, without evaluating all the pairs.
3. CONFIRM BY PART OF SPEECH. Swapped words are nearly always the same part of speech as each other — noun with noun, verb with verb, adjective with adjective. If your candidate pair is a noun and a verb, you are probably wrong. This rule alone kills half the option list and costs two seconds.
4. Substitute the pair and read ONLY the two affected phrases, not the whole sentence. If both now collocate naturally with their neighbours, mark it.
5. If no word looks obviously wrong on the first read, go to the option list and test pairs that share a part of speech, starting with the pair whose two contexts are most similar.
6. Mark 'no interchange required' only after confirming all four bold words collocate with their immediate neighbours.
7. The moment you find one clean pair, STOP. Do not verify the others. IBPS builds exactly one correct interchange.
tricks: Check each bold word against the word IMMEDIATELY beside it, not against the sentence as a whole. Word swap is collocation: 'make a decision' / 'take a decision' / 'heavy traffic' / 'strong tea' / 'commit a crime' / 'pose a threat'. A bold word that does not pair with its neighbour is the misplaced one, and this local check is roughly four times faster than reading the sentence again.

Scan for the SHAPE-MATCHED pair before reading for meaning. Two bold words that are both abstract nouns, both '-ing' forms, or both comparative adjectives are prime swap candidates. You can often spot the pair in five seconds on shape alone and then confirm on meaning.

You do not need to understand the sentence's topic. Word swap questions on macroeconomics, marine ecology or constitutional law are exactly as solvable as ones about traffic. Never skip a word swap for unfamiliar subject matter — this is free marks that aspirants throw away out of intimidation.
If a bold word sits directly after 'a' or 'an', check sound agreement. A mismatched article exposes the misplaced word instantly and requires no vocabulary at all.
A and D swap as often as adjacent pairs do. Do not assume the misplaced words are near each other — the setter deliberately separates them because distance makes the nonsense harder to hear.
traps: Swapping the two words that are semantically related — two economics terms, two weather words — merely because they feel connected. Topical relatedness is not evidence of misplacement, and this is the most common wrong answer.
Trying to relocate three words. Exactly two move.
Re-reading the whole sentence three or four times. One full read plus one targeted collocation check is the entire budget.
Missing the 'no interchange required' option and forcing a swap because the format seems to demand one.
Assuming the bold words must be swapped in the order they appear.
Over-thinking a sentence on an unfamiliar topic. The topic is irrelevant to the method — if you are thinking about the subject matter, you have left the technique.
Reading the swapped version of the whole sentence to verify. Read only the two repaired phrases; full re-reading costs 10 seconds per question across a 5-question Mains block.
e-wordswap.timeTarget: 20-25 seconds per question in Prelims; 25-30 seconds in Mains where sentences are longer. A 5-question Mains block should close in 2 to 2.5 minutes.
e-wordswap.masteryCheck: You spot the misplaced word within 8 seconds of a single read, and complete 10 word-swap questions in 4 minutes with 9 correct — and for each you can name the collocation that was broken.

e-wordrearr.whatItIs: A sentence containing several blanks with a set of words labelled (A)-(E) to be placed into them. Questions ask which word occupies a given position, or for the correct sequence. It is solved entirely by grammatical slot-typing, not by meaning.
e-wordrearr.coreMethod:
1. Read the sentence frame — the FIXED text around the blanks. The fixed words, not the movable ones, determine the answer.
2. For each blank, read the word immediately before and immediately after it and write down the grammatical type that slot demands. This slot-typing is the entire method.
3. TYPE EACH MOVABLE WORD by its suffix, which takes about five seconds for all five: -tion / -ity / -ness / -ment / -ance = noun; -ate / -ise / -ify / -en = verb; -ous / -ful / -ive / -al / -ic / -able = adjective; -ly = adverb. Words without a telling suffix get typed by meaning.
4. Place the MOST RESTRICTED words first — a past participle, a preposition, an '-ly' adverb, a word that only fits one slot. Never start with a common noun; nouns fit many slots and starting there guarantees rework.
5. Two or three words will have exactly one legal slot each. Place those, then the remaining one or two fall out by elimination and are confirmed by meaning.
6. Verify subject-verb agreement across the completed sentence. A plural subject taking a singular verb means you have mis-slotted.
7. Answer only the position actually asked.
tricks: Fixed-text articles and prepositions are your strongest hooks and they cost nothing to read: a blank after 'the' needs a noun or adjective; after 'to' needs a base verb or a noun; after 'very' needs an adjective or adverb; after 'has/have/had' needs a past participle; after 'is/are being' needs a past participle.
Suffix-typing all five words before touching the sentence takes five seconds and eliminates most of the search space. Do it as a fixed opening move every time.

If the question asks only 'which word comes at position 3', you often do not need the full arrangement. Type the words, pin position 3 from its adjacent fixed text, and check against the options. This can halve the time on a 5-question set.

In a 5-question set built on the same sentence family, solve the arrangement ONCE properly and then answer all five positional questions from it. Aspirants routinely re-solve for each question and lose 90 seconds.
The tense marker in the fixed text (has / was / will be) determines which verb form goes where. Find it before placing any verb.
traps: Solving the entire sentence when only one position is asked. Read the question stem first.
Confusing this with word swap. Here ALL the labelled words move into blanks; in word swap only two move and there are no blanks. Diagnosing the format wrong costs the whole question.
Forgetting that '-ing' forms can be gerunds functioning as nouns ('swimming is healthy'), not verbs. Mistyping a gerund as a verb misroutes two words at once.
Skimming the fixed text. The movable words are the visible part of the puzzle but the fixed text holds the answer.
Placing the nouns first because they are easiest to understand. Nouns are the least constrained and must go last.
Not re-checking agreement after the final placement — the last word placed is the one most likely to break it.
e-wordrearr.timeTarget: 25-35 seconds per question; a 5-question set built on the same sentence in 2 to 2.5 minutes total once you stop re-solving per question.
e-wordrearr.masteryCheck: You can suffix-type all five movable words in under 10 seconds and place them correctly in under 30 seconds, on 8 of 10 questions — and on a 5-question set you solve the arrangement once and answer all five from it.

e-wordusage.whatItIs: One word is given and used in three separate sentences (I, II, III). You identify which sentences use it correctly. Almost always exactly one question in the paper — a fast mark or a slow trap depending entirely on whether you run the checks in the right order.
e-wordusage.coreMethod:
1. Establish the word's PART OF SPEECH in each sentence first, before considering meaning at all. The commonest error IBPS plants is a noun used as a verb or the reverse — advice/advise, practice/practise, effect/affect, licence/license. Check the slot, not the dictionary.
2. Check the word's FIXED PREPOSITION or collocation in each sentence. A right meaning with a wrong preposition is still wrong usage. Comprise takes no 'of'. Discuss takes no 'about'. Dispose takes 'of'. Bestow takes 'on/upon'. Deprive takes 'of'. Consist takes 'of'. Result takes 'in' or 'from' with different meanings.
3. Check SENSE. Many test words carry two or three legitimate senses and IBPS deploys a plausible fourth that the word does not actually have. Ask whether this specific sense exists, not whether the sentence sounds acceptable.
4. Record a yes/no verdict for each of the three sentences BEFORE reading the options. Deciding first and matching second prevents the options from steering you.
5. Match your three verdicts to the option list.
6. If you are unsure on exactly one sentence, read the options to find the DISCRIMINATOR — often only one sentence separates the surviving options, so spend your remaining seconds only on that sentence and ignore the settled ones.
tricks: Run the part-of-speech test first, always. It resolves the majority of word-usage questions in seconds and requires no vocabulary depth whatsoever — you are checking grammar, not knowledge.
If the same collocation appears in two of the three sentences, those two stand or fall together. Treat them as a single unit and you have reduced a three-way judgement to a two-way one.

Read the options before finalising all three sentences. Frequently two sentences are agreed across every option and only one is contested; identify the contested sentence and spend your time only there.

The words IBPS recycles here are common words with many senses, not rare words: bear, hold, run, draw, set, take, keep, address, table, board, subject, present, object, count, record, issue, charge, order, place, mark. Expect an everyday word doing an unfamiliar job.

If a sentence reads perfectly naturally on the first pass, it is almost certainly correct. Planted errors in this format are glaring once you look for the right thing — trust fluency here more than you would in phrase replacement.
traps: Deciding a sentence is wrong because it sounds formal or unfamiliar. Formal register is not error, and this is where most marks in this format are lost.
Judging on meaning alone and walking past a preposition violation.
Missing that the target word appears in a different FORM across the three sentences — 'bear' may show up as 'bore' or 'borne', and the inflection itself may be the planted error.
Marking 'all three are correct' as a default because checking three sentences feels expensive. It is genuinely correct sometimes, but only mark it after three verdicts, not instead of them.
Spending 60 or 90 seconds on a single-mark question. Cap it at 40 seconds and move — the opportunity cost inside a 20-minute clock is two fillers.
Assuming the given word's most familiar sense is the only one being tested. The question exists precisely because the word has several.
e-wordusage.timeTarget: 25-35 seconds per question, hard-capped at 40. It is worth one mark and should never be allowed to run long.
e-wordusage.masteryCheck: You can classify all three sentences as correct or incorrect WITH A STATED REASON — part of speech, preposition, or sense — in under 30 seconds total, on 8 of 10 questions.
