e-oddone.topicName: Odd one out and spelling error
e-oddone.whatItIs: Two related formats. The spelling/inappropriate-word type gives a sentence with four bold words and asks which is wrongly spelt or contextually wrong, with 'All Correct' as the fifth option. The odd-one-out type gives four or five statements sharing a context and asks which does not belong.
e-oddone.coreMethod:
SPELLING / INAPPROPRIATE WORD:
1. Scan the four bold words for SPELLING in isolation first, before reading the sentence at all. Spelling is recognised, not reasoned — this pass takes five seconds and often ends the question.
2. Check double letters first: accommodate, occurrence, embarrass, committee, harass, necessary. Then check -ence/-ance and -ible/-able endings. These two families cover most planted spelling errors.
3. If all four are correctly spelt, NOW read the sentence and check contextual appropriateness. This is where the format hides its real difficulty — a correctly spelt word can be entirely the wrong word.
4. For appropriateness, check part of speech first: advice/advise, practice/practise, effect/affect, principal/principle, complement/compliment, stationary/stationery, eminent/imminent, adapt/adopt, elicit/illicit, discreet/discrete, counsel/council, canvas/canvass, moral/morale, personal/personnel, loose/lose.
5. Only after both passes may you mark 'All Correct'.

ODD ONE OUT:
1. Read all statements and name the shared theme in three or four words.
2. The intruder typically shifts the SUBJECT ENTITY, shifts the time frame or tense, states an evaluation of the opposite sign, or is a general definition sitting among specific claims.
3. Apply the LINKAGE test, which is more reliable than theme-matching: the four belonging statements will chain into a paragraph through shared nouns, pronouns and connectors. The intruder links to none of them. Try to pair each statement with another — the one with no partner is the answer.
4. You are not looking for the statement that is wrong or that you disagree with. You are looking for the one that is about something else.
tricks: Do the four-word spelling scan before reading the sentence. Most aspirants read the sentence first and burn 10 seconds recovering information they did not need.

Memorise the recurring misspelling set — banks recycle it relentlessly: accommodation, occurrence, embarrass, harass, privilege, recommend, separate, definitely, maintenance, questionnaire, entrepreneur, liaison, bureaucracy, conscience, committee, necessary, occasion, achievement, receive, existence, government, independent, environment, restaurant, rhythm, colleague, foreign, immediately, beginning, successful, acknowledgement, consensus, millennium, supersede.
Memorise the confusable-pairs list — roughly 40 pairs cover almost everything IBPS asks in the 'inappropriate word' version, and this is where the harder marks in this format sit.
For odd one out, the fastest single test is: which statement has a different grammatical SUBJECT from the others? Scan subjects only. Fifteen seconds.

In odd one out, if two statements both look odd, the true intruder is the one that cannot be placed ANYWHERE in a valid ordering — the other one will fit somewhere. Try placing each and the answer resolves.
Tense-frame shift is a strong intruder signal: four statements in present tense and one in past narrative usually identifies itself.
traps: Marking 'All Correct' too readily. IBPS plants an error in roughly four out of five of these questions, so a high 'All Correct' rate means you are under-checking.
Checking spelling only and never running the appropriateness pass. The contextually-wrong-but-correctly-spelt word is the format's main weapon and it is invisible if you stop after the spelling scan.

Marking British spellings as errors. IBPS uses British conventions — colour, realise, programme, centre, labour, defence — and does NOT test the British/American difference as a mistake. Do not mark 'organise' wrong.
In odd one out, choosing the statement you disagree with, or the one that seems least important. Neither opinion nor importance is the criterion; only linkage is.
In odd one out, choosing the most general statement — general statements are frequently the topic sentence and belong.
Confusing odd-one-out with coherent-paragraph. In odd one out you only remove; in coherent paragraph you remove AND order. Read the stem.
Spending more than 20 seconds on a spelling question. It is the fastest question type in the paper and should be treated as such.
e-oddone.timeTarget: 15-20 seconds per spelling/inappropriate-word question — the fastest format in the English section. 35-45 seconds per odd-one-out question, which is a genuinely different animal.
e-oddone.masteryCheck: On 10 misspelt-word questions you score 9 in under 3 minutes, AND you can write out 30 of the standard confusable pairs (affect/effect type) from memory with both meanings — the memory test, not the quiz score, is the real check.

e-idioms.whatItIs: An idiom is given, either standalone or embedded in a sentence, and you choose its meaning — or an idiom appears as one of the options in a phrase replacement or fillers question. Low direct weightage at Clerk level, but idioms leak into several other formats.
e-idioms.coreMethod:
1. Do not attempt to memorise a thousand idioms. Learn the roughly 150 that bank exams recycle, grouped by theme — money and business, time and urgency, difficulty and failure, success, relationships, communication, secrecy. Thematic grouping roughly doubles retention over alphabetical lists.
2. When you meet an idiom you know, answer in five seconds and move. Recognition questions should not be reasoned.
3. When you meet one you do not know, decode in this order:
   (a) POLARITY. Read the surrounding sentence and decide whether the required meaning is positive or negative. Kill every option with the wrong sign — this typically removes three of five.
   (b) LITERAL IMAGE. What picture do the words paint, and what human situation does that picture suggest? 'Burn the midnight oil' pictures working by lamplight. The image is often a usable clue even when the idiom is unfamiliar.
   (c) GRAMMATICAL SLOT. An idiom functioning as a verb phrase needs an option that is a verb phrase. Options of the wrong shape are wrong.
4. Reject any option that is simply a literal restatement of the idiom's words. Idioms are non-literal by definition, so the literal option is always a distractor.
5. If two options share the correct polarity, choose the one whose INTENSITY matches the sentence.
6. Apply the guessing rule: with 0.25 negative marking, guess only if you have eliminated at least two options. Otherwise leave it — one idiom is not worth the variance.
tricks: Polarity-matching alone converts an unknown idiom into a 1-in-2 or 1-in-3 in about ten seconds. Read the sentence, decide the sign, strike the wrong-sign options. This is the single technique that makes unknown idioms answerable.
Learn idioms INSIDE example sentences, never as a bare two-column list. In the exam you will always meet them in context, and context-learnt idioms are retrieved far faster than list-learnt ones.

Business and money idioms are over-represented in bank exams — prioritise: in the red, make ends meet, cut corners, a tall order, call the shots, the ball is in your court, bite the bullet, on the back burner, get the axe, cash cow, tighten the belt, turn a blind eye, go the extra mile, in the same boat, beat around the bush, once in a blue moon, at the drop of a hat, hit the nail on the head, burn the midnight oil, steal someone's thunder, break the ice, keep at bay, on thin ice, a blessing in disguise, bring to the table.

If the idiom contains a body part or an animal, it is almost certainly in the standard recycled list. Recognise it or skip it within five seconds rather than reasoning about it — reasoning about a fixed expression you have simply never seen does not work.

Do idioms as spaced revision during dead time — commute, queues, before sleep — never as a dedicated 60-minute block. The weightage does not justify prime study hours, and memorisation works better distributed anyway.
traps: Choosing the literal meaning. This is the entire trap of the topic and the option is always present.

Confusing near-identical idioms: call it a day vs call it quits; on the cards vs in the cards; take for granted vs take for a ride; pull one's leg vs pull one's socks up; make up vs make out; put up with vs put up to.
Translating from a similar-sounding Hindi idiom. Several map to genuinely different meanings and the false-friend feels convincing.
Spending 60 seconds on a one-mark idiom you do not know. Polarity-eliminate, and either guess with two options gone or leave it.
Guessing blind. At 0.25 negative marking a blind five-way guess has an expected value of exactly zero — it adds variance and no marks.
Over-investing in this topic because idiom lists feel like productive studying. They are the most satisfying and least efficient English preparation available at Clerk level.

e-matchcol.whatItIs: Two columns of sentence fragments — Column I with items A, B, C and Column II with items D, E, F. You match them to form grammatically and contextually correct sentences. Crucially, not every item must find a partner: 'may or may not connect' is part of the standard instruction.
e-matchcol.coreMethod:
1. Read the instruction line. Confirm whether unmatched items are permitted — in the IBPS version they are, and assuming a complete one-to-one matching is the format's principal trap.
2. Do NOT test all nine combinations. Start from the item with the MOST grammatical constraint: the one ending in a preposition, a relative pronoun, an incomplete verb phrase, or a conjunction.
3. Read only the EDGES. For each Column I item, note the last two or three words. For each Column II item, note the first two or three words. You are matching junctions, not reading sentences — this is the difference between a 40-second question and a 90-second one.
4. Apply grammar filters at the junction, in this order: (a) subject-verb agreement across the join, (b) tense compatibility, (c) preposition or article completion, (d) number agreement of any pronoun crossing the join.
5. Then apply a two-second sense check. The completed sentence must be sensible, not merely legal — the standard distractor is a join that is grammatically flawless and semantically absurd.
6. USE THE OPTIONS TO CONSTRAIN. Find the ONE match you are most confident about and eliminate every option that does not contain it. Frequently a single confident match determines the whole answer without your evaluating the other two.
7. Answer the question actually asked — some sets ask only which single pairing is valid, not the full mapping.
tricks: Read only the junction words. The last three words of a Column I item and the first three of a Column II item contain everything that decides the match. Reading all six items in full costs 40 seconds you do not have inside a 20-minute clock.

The relative-pronoun test is the fastest single filter: if a Column I item ends with 'which', 'who' or 'that', the matching Column II item must begin with a VERB, not with a subject. This kills most candidates instantly.
Number agreement across the join: a Column I item ending in a plural noun demands a plural verb at the start of its partner. Scan for singular/plural mismatch before reading meaning at all.

Attack the option list first. If every option contains 'B-D', then B-D is free and you only have to decide A and C — you have converted a nine-combination problem into a four-combination one before doing any grammar.

When two candidate matches both work grammatically, the wrong one is nearly always the one that is semantically absurd rather than the one that is semantically dull. Correct matches in this format tend to produce ordinary, unremarkable sentences.
traps: Assuming a complete one-to-one matching. IBPS explicitly allows items to go unmatched, so 'only A-E' is a legal and frequently correct answer. Forcing three matches is the commonest way this question is lost.
Matching on topic similarity instead of grammar. Two halves about the same subject can be grammatically incapable of joining.
Reading all six items in full before starting. Junction-only reading is not a shortcut, it is the method.
Missing a subject-verb disagreement because the join falls mid-clause and the disagreement is not audible.
Not checking that the completed sentence contains exactly one main verb — a join can produce two main verbs with no conjunction and still sound acceptable at speed.
Solving all three matches when the question asks for only one valid pairing.
e-matchcol.timeTarget: 30-40 seconds per question when it is a 3-question set built on the same columns, so roughly 2 minutes for the whole set. Reading the columns is a fixed cost paid once — which is exactly why you must not re-read them for each question.
e-matchcol.masteryCheck: You complete a 3-item match-the-column set in under 2 minutes with all three correct, deciding every match on junction words alone — and you can state, for each rejected pairing, whether it failed on agreement, tense, preposition or sense.

e-connectors.whatItIs: Two separate statements are given and you choose the connector or opening phrase that combines them into one sentence without changing the meaning. The 'starters' variant offers three candidate openings (A, B, C) and asks which of them can begin the combined sentence.
e-connectors.coreMethod:
1. Before reading any option, name the LOGICAL RELATION between the two statements. There are only six possibilities and naming it in one word is the whole game: contrast, cause-to-effect, effect-to-cause, addition, condition, time.
2. Pull the connector family that matches:
   - Contrast: although, though, even though, whereas, while, despite / in spite of, however, nevertheless, yet, notwithstanding
   - Cause to effect: so, therefore, thus, hence, consequently, as a result, and so
   - Effect to cause: because, since, as, owing to, due to, on account of, inasmuch as
   - Addition: moreover, besides, in addition, not only...but also, as well as, furthermore
   - Condition: if, unless, provided that, in case, lest, on condition that
   - Time: when, while, before, after, as soon as, no sooner...than, hardly/scarcely...when, once
3. Apply the CLAUSE-VERSUS-NOUN RULE, which is the fastest filter in the topic and decides most questions before meaning is considered. 'Despite / in spite of / owing to / due to / because of / on account of' must be followed by a NOUN or an -ING form, never by a clause. 'Although / because / since / while / as' must be followed by a CLAUSE with its own subject and verb. So 'Despite he was tired' is wrong and 'Despite being tired' is right.
4. Check the DOUBLE-CONNECTOR BAN. English uses one connector per join. 'Although... but...', 'Because... so...', 'Though... yet...' as a pair are all wrong in exam English. Scan every option for this before anything else — it is a three-second sweep that kills options outright.
5. Check INVERSION requirements. 'No sooner had he...', 'Hardly had he...when', 'Scarcely had he...when', 'Not only did he...but also' all demand an inverted clause. If the option uses these and the following clause is not inverted, it is wrong.
6. Verify meaning is preserved and that cause and effect have not been reversed.
7. FOR STARTERS: evaluate each of A, B and C independently and record a yes/no for each, then match to the option combinations. Do not evaluate them as a group.
8. Read the combined sentence once before marking.
tricks: The clause-versus-noun rule alone decides the majority of connector questions and takes about four seconds. Check what grammatical unit follows the connector in each option before you consider what any option means.

Sweep for double connectors first. Any option pairing 'Although...but', 'Because...therefore', 'Since...so' is dead on arrival regardless of meaning. Setters include one or two of these in almost every question.

Identify which statement carries the MAIN idea. In the correct combination that statement stays as the main clause and the other becomes subordinate. Getting this the wrong way round produces a grammatically fine sentence that says the wrong thing — which is exactly the trap.
'Lest' is always followed by 'should' or a bare subjunctive and NEVER by 'not' — 'lest he should fall', never 'lest he should not fall'. This exact plant recurs.
'While' means both 'during' and 'whereas'. If a question seems to have two valid time-connectors, check whether 'while' is actually being used for contrast.
In the starters format, 'all three' is a genuinely correct option often enough that you must test each phrase, but it is also the lazy default — force yourself to write three separate verdicts.
traps: Choosing a connector that is grammatically legal but reverses cause and effect. Always identify which statement is the reason and which is the result before selecting.
Missing that 'due to' properly modifies a NOUN while 'because of' and 'owing to' modify a clause or verb — a recurring Mains-level plant that most aspirants have never been taught.
Ignoring comma placement, which signals whether the connector opens the sentence or joins mid-sentence and sometimes disqualifies an otherwise valid option.
Assuming 'while' always signals time.
In starters, marking 'all three' without three separate tests.
Selecting a connector that subtly strengthens or weakens the original claim. The instruction says without changing the meaning, and an option that turns a correlation into a causation has changed it.
Treating this as a vocabulary topic. It is a rules topic with about a dozen rules, which is why it is one of the fastest topics to take from zero to reliable.
e-connectors.timeTarget: 25-35 seconds per connector question; 30-40 seconds per starters question, since three candidate phrases must each be tested.
e-connectors.masteryCheck: You can name the logical relation between two statements within 5 seconds, and you eliminate options using the clause-versus-noun rule and the double-connector ban BEFORE reading their meanings — scoring 8 of 10 in under 5 minutes.

e-paracompletion.whatItIs: A short paragraph with one sentence missing — usually the last, sometimes the middle or first — and five candidate sentences. You choose the one that completes it coherently. It is one of the slower English formats and must be triaged accordingly.
e-paracompletion.coreMethod:
1. Read the paragraph and identify its DIRECTION in the last complete sentence before the blank. Is the argument building toward a conclusion, an illustration, a contrast, a consequence, or a qualification? Name it.
2. Read the word immediately before the blank, and if the blank is mid-paragraph, the sentence immediately after it. A mid-paragraph blank must connect in BOTH directions, and aspirants routinely check only backwards.
3. PREDICT the missing sentence's content in your own words before reading any option. This is the load-bearing step — without a prediction you will be steered by whichever option sounds most impressive.
4. Eliminate options that: introduce a topic mentioned nowhere in the paragraph; contradict the paragraph's established tone; merely repeat information already stated; are far broader or more universal than the paragraph's scope; or are grammatically disconnected — a pronoun with no antecedent, a tense that clashes.
5. Prefer the option that picks up the LAST-MENTIONED specific noun or idea. Paragraph flow is chain-like: the end of each sentence sets up the start of the next.
6. Read the last complete sentence together with your chosen option. They must read as one continuous thought, not two adjacent true statements.
tricks: Scan the options for the KEY NOUN from the sentence immediately preceding the blank, or a pronoun standing for it. Often only one option contains it, and that is your answer in ten seconds without full analysis.

If the blank is the LAST sentence, the answer is a conclusion, consequence, or forward-looking implication — not a new fact. Eliminate on sight any option introducing fresh factual content, which usually removes two.
If the blank is the FIRST sentence, the answer must be general, must introduce the topic, and must contain no backward-referring pronouns. The reverse test.

Kill options opening with 'However' or 'But' unless the paragraph genuinely sets up a contrast immediately before the blank. Setters include a contrast option in most questions precisely because it sounds sophisticated.
Extreme quantifiers in an option — always, never, no one, entirely, completely, must — usually mark it wrong. Bank paragraph-completion answers are moderate in tone.
If you are behind pace inside the 20-minute clock, this is a legitimate topic to skip entirely. At 40-50 seconds a question it costs the equivalent of two and a half fillers.
traps: Choosing the option that is TRUE in the real world rather than the one that fits THIS paragraph. This is the dominant error and it feels like good judgement while you are making it.
Choosing the longest, most detailed option. Correct completions are usually plain and short; length reads as substance and is manufactured to.
Ignoring the sentence AFTER the blank when the blank is mid-paragraph. The answer must connect forwards as well as backwards, and checking only one direction leaves two options standing.
Choosing an option that answers a question the paragraph never asked.
Being pulled by an option that echoes the paragraph's own words verbatim. Repetition is not completion — a completion must ADD the next step.
Treating this like reading comprehension and re-reading the paragraph three times. One careful read plus a prediction is the budget.
e-paracompletion.timeTarget: 40-50 seconds per question. This is among the slowest English formats — treat it as a considered attempt, not a quick one, and be willing to skip it under time pressure.
e-paracompletion.masteryCheck: You predict the missing sentence's content in your own words before reading the options, and your prediction matches the core idea of the correct option on 7 of 10 questions. Score alone does not verify mastery here — the prediction hit rate does.

e-coherent.whatItIs: Five sentences are given; one does not belong, and the other four form a coherent paragraph. You may be asked which sentence is the intruder, and/or the correct order of the remaining four. It is odd-one-out and para jumble fused into one set.
e-coherent.coreMethod:
1. Read the question stem FIRST. Some sets ask only for the intruder, some ask for positions too. Ordering four sentences you did not need to order is a 40-second waste.
2. Read all five and name the theme in three to five words.
3. FIND THE INTRUDER BEFORE ORDERING ANYTHING. This is the correct order of operations and reversing it is the format's main time trap — ordering five sentences when one does not belong produces a mess you then have to unpick.
4. Identify the intruder by LEXICAL CHAINING, which is more reliable than judging theme: underline the key noun in each sentence. Four sentences will share nouns, pronouns or referents forming a chain. One will be lexically isolated — no shared content word with any other sentence. That is your answer, and the scan takes about fifteen seconds.
5. Secondary intruder signals: a different grammatical subject from the others; a time-frame or tense shift (four in present, one in past narrative); a claim of a different KIND, such as a policy recommendation sitting among historical facts.
6. Once the intruder is removed, order the remaining four using standard para-jumble technique — opener disqualifiers, pronoun-antecedent pairs, indefinite-to-definite article progression, connectors.
7. Read the final four in order. If they flow and reinserting the removed sentence anywhere breaks the flow, you are right.
tricks: Lexical isolation is the fastest test available and it requires no comprehension: scan the NOUNS only, ignoring everything else. The sentence sharing no content word with any other is the intruder. Fifteen seconds for a mark that others spend ninety seconds on.

If two sentences both look odd, the true intruder is the one that cannot be placed ANYWHERE in a valid ordering. Try slotting each into the remaining chain — the other one will fit somewhere and reveal itself.
Never order first. Removing the intruder first turns a five-item ordering problem into a four-item one, which is materially easier because there are fewer false pairs.
If the question asks only for the intruder, do not order at all. Read the stem, answer it, move on.
Tense-frame shift is a strong and very quick signal — scan only the main verbs of the five sentences and check whether one sits in a different time frame.
traps: Removing the sentence that seems least important or least interesting. Importance is not the criterion; lexical and logical linkage is.
Removing the most general sentence. General sentences are frequently the topic sentence and belong at the head of the paragraph.
Ordering first and then hunting for the misfit. This reverses the efficient order of operations and roughly doubles the time.
Forgetting that the set may ask for BOTH the intruder and positions — check the stem before you start, not after.
Confusing this with plain odd-one-out, where the five statements are standalone and never need ordering. Here four must chain into a single paragraph, so linkage matters more than theme.
Attempting this set early in the section. It is a multi-question set with a slow first step; place it after your fast formats are banked.
e-coherent.timeTarget: 60-90 seconds for the whole set including intruder identification and ordering — roughly 30-45 seconds per mark on a 2-3 question set. Intruder alone, if that is all that is asked: 30-40 seconds.
e-coherent.masteryCheck: You identify the intruder in a five-sentence coherent-paragraph set in under 40 seconds using lexical chaining alone, on 8 of 10 sets — and you can point to the specific shared noun or pronoun linking each of the four belonging sentences.
questionPatterns: Five sentences A-E; one does not belong; questions ask both the intruder and the order of the rest

e-inference.whatItIs: Questions asking what follows from a passage without being stated in it — either inside a reading comprehension set, or as standalone short statements with five candidate inferences. It is the lowest-accuracy question type in the English section and must be triaged, not attacked.
e-inference.coreMethod:
1. Get the definitions straight, because misreading the stem is the top cause of loss here. An INFERENCE must be true given the passage but is not stated in it. An ASSUMPTION is something the author took for granted before writing. A CONCLUSION is the passage's own final claim. A STATED FACT is a paraphrase of the text. These four stems demand different behaviours and the same option can be right for one and wrong for another.
2. Locate the target region. Inference questions almost always aim at a specific two-to-four line stretch, not the whole passage. Take a distinctive keyword from the question stem and find it in the text.
3. Read that region and state, in your own words, what MUST follow. Do this before reading the options.
4. Eliminate in this fixed order, because it is ordered fastest-first:
   (a) TOO STRONG — the option contains all, never, only, must, proves, entirely, no one, cannot. Almost always out. This is a wording scan, not a comprehension task, and it kills two or three options in under ten seconds.
   (b) OUT OF SCOPE — the option raises something the passage never discusses. Out.
   (c) REVERSED — the option states the causal direction backwards. Out.
   (d) RESTATEMENT — the option copies the passage with light rewording. Out for 'can be inferred', but CORRECT for 'is stated'. Re-read the stem before applying this one.
   (e) UNSUPPORTED COMPARISON — the option claims X exceeds Y when the passage compares nothing. Out.
5. What survives should be modest and hedged — may, is likely to, suggests, tends to. Pick it.
6. Never import outside knowledge. If a statement is true in the real world but unsupported by the passage, it is wrong.
7. TRIAGE: if two options survive elimination and you cannot separate them within 20 more seconds, leave the question. Industry data puts aspirant accuracy on inference questions near 60% against 85%+ on fact and vocabulary questions — a coin-flip attempt with 0.25 negative marking is a bad trade when faster marks are still on the table.
tricks: Scan the option WORDING for absolutes before reading any option for content. All / never / only / must / entirely / proves. This single ten-second sweep eliminates two to three options on most inference questions and is the highest-value habit in the topic.
Correct inference options tend to be the SHORTEST and most hedged. Long, specific, confident options are manufactured to look authoritative and are usually distractors.
Read the stem twice. 'Can be inferred' and 'is stated in the passage' demand opposite treatment of a paraphrase option, and confusing them is the single most expensive error in RC.

Anchor to the author's TONE. If the author is cautiously positive, an option expressing strong criticism is out on tone alone regardless of its content — you can reject it without evaluating the logic.

For standalone statement-inference questions, ask of each option: 'what else would I have to believe for this to follow?' If the answer is 'nothing', that is the inference. If you must supply a bridging belief, it is not.

Within an RC set, do the vocabulary and fact questions FIRST and the inference questions LAST. Vocabulary questions need no passage reading and take ten seconds; inference questions take fifty. Doing them in printed order is why aspirants run out of time mid-passage.
traps: Using real-world knowledge. The most common and most expensive error in the topic, and it feels like intelligence rather than error while you are doing it.
Choosing an option because it is mentioned in the passage. Mentioned is not inferred — for an inference stem, a faithful paraphrase is a wrong answer.
Missing a negation in either the passage line or the option. One 'not' inverts everything and tired eyes drop it.
Selecting an option that IS a valid inference, but from a different part of the passage than the one the question targets. Setters plant these deliberately.
Choosing the option that sounds most intelligent. Inference answers are deliberately unimpressive.
Spending 90 seconds on one inference question inside a 20-minute sectional clock. That is two fillers and a spelling question forgone for a coin flip.

Treating Prelims and Mains identically here. In Prelims, RC is 8-9 of 30 with short passages and inference questions are skippable. In Mains, RC is 16-18 of 40 and inference cannot be avoided at that volume — the same question type deserves different treatment in the two papers.
e-inference.timeTarget: 45-60 seconds per question — the slowest question type in the English section. In Prelims, cap at 50 seconds and skip. In Mains, where RC is 16-18 of 40 marks, allow the full 60 and accept it as a necessary cost.
e-inference.masteryCheck: On 10 inference questions you eliminate at least three options per question using the scope, strength and direction tests within 20 seconds, and score 7 of 10 — and for every answer you can quote the exact passage line that supports it. If you cannot point to the line, the answer was a guess even when it was right.

e-inference.blockPlan: 15m concept: take one editorial and, for each paragraph, write one statement that IS inferable and one that is merely stated — producing the distinction yourself is what makes it stick, and it cannot be absorbed by reading a rule. 20m untimed: one RC passage where for every inference question you quote the supporting line and label each wrong option with its elimination category (too strong / out of scope / reversed / restatement / unsupported comparison). No line quoted means it counts as wrong. 20m timed: two RC passages in 18 minutes, doing vocabulary questions first, fact questions second, inference last, and deliberately skipping any inference question still unresolved at 60 seconds. 5m error log: track how often you chose a real-world-true option and how often you misread the stem. Those two causes account for most inference losses and both are fixable by discipline rather than by study.
